[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 020201] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a nonparametric learning method for continuous-variable quantum states using tomographic representations.
motivation: Traditional representations of continuous-variable quantum states are often impractical; tomographic pictures offer an accessible alternative but require efficient learning algorithms.
method: Develops a nonparametric approach based on kernel methods and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces to learn the tomographic representation from measurement data.
result: Demonstrates that the method can accurately reconstruct non-Gaussian quantum states, including those with negativity in the Wigner function, from limited samples.
conclusion: The nonparametric learning framework provides a practical tool for characterizing continuous-variable quantum states, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Entanglement Growth From Entangled States: A Unified Perspective On Entanglement Generation And Transport
authors: Chun-Yue Zhang, Zi-Xiang Li, And Shi-Xin Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Chun-Yue Zhang, Zi-Xiang Li, and Shi-Xin Zhang

Studies of entanglement dynamics in quantum many-body systems have focused largely on initial product states. Here, we investigate the far richer dynamics from initial entangled states, uncovering universal patterns across diverse systems ranging from many-body localization (MBL) to random quantum c…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 020404] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement dynamics from initial entangled states in many-body systems, revealing universal patterns across MBL and random quantum circuits.
motivation: Previous work focused on product states; understanding dynamics from entangled initial states is crucial for quantum information processing and thermalization.
method: The authors numerically simulate entanglement growth using tensor network methods and analyze scaling behavior in MBL and random circuit models.
result: They find that entanglement growth from entangled states exhibits a universal crossover from ballistic to logarithmic growth, depending on the initial entanglement structure.
conclusion: Initial entanglement significantly alters entanglement dynamics, providing a unified framework for entanglement generation and transport.

title: Metacavity Quantum Electrodynamics
authors: Xueshi Li (李学诗), Ziwei Wang (王子维), Yan Chen (陈岩), Dong Liu ((刘栋), Kaili Xiong (熊凯莉), Guangfeng Wang (王光丰), Jiantao Ma (马剑涛), Ying Yu (喻颖), Jiawei Wang (王嘉威), Zhanling Wang (王占领), Xiao Li (李霄), Xianfeng Chen (陈险峰), Erez Hasman, Bo Wang (王波), Jin Liu (刘进), And Tian Jiang
abstract:
Author(s): Xueshi Li (李学诗), Ziwei Wang (王子维), Yan Chen (陈岩), Dong Liu ((刘栋), Kaili Xiong (熊凯莉), Guangfeng Wang (王光丰), Jiantao Ma (马剑涛), Ying Yu (喻颖), Jiawei Wang (王嘉威), Zhanling Wang (王占领), Xiao Li (李霄), Xianfeng Chen (陈险峰), Erez Hasman, Bo Wang (王波), Jin Liu (刘进), and Tian Jiang (江天)

Cavity quantum electrodynamics (cQED) harnesses light-matter interactions to produce nonclassical light states. However, a fundamental challenge lies in simultaneously achieving Purcell enhancement and tailored wave front control within a single cavity, due to conflicting resonator requirements. Her…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 023601] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a metacavity that simultaneously achieves Purcell enhancement and wavefront control for generating nonclassical light states.
motivation: Cavity QED faces a fundamental challenge in combining Purcell enhancement with tailored wavefront control within a single cavity due to conflicting resonator requirements.
method: The authors design a metacavity integrating a photonic crystal cavity with a metasurface to achieve both high Purcell factor and arbitrary wavefront shaping.
result: They experimentally demonstrate enhanced spontaneous emission and controlled emission directionality, producing nonclassical light with tailored spatial properties.
conclusion: The metacavity approach overcomes the traditional trade-off in cQED, enabling new capabilities for quantum light sources and quantum networks.

title: Unbounded Sequence Of Observers Exhibiting Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen Steering Via Probabilistic Projective Measurements
authors: Yan-Hong Song, Bang-Hai Wang, Zhi-Hua Chen, Zhihao Ma, And Hui-Juan Zuo
abstract:
Author(s): Yan-Hong Song, Bang-Hai Wang, Zhi-Hua Chen, Zhihao Ma, and Hui-Juan Zuo

Recent studies have demonstrated that coherent weak measurements allow Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering to be shared sequentially between a single Alice and multiple Bobs. Theoretically, this permits an unbounded sequence in the high-dimensional limit. In this work, we investigate whether the experi…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012411] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering can be shared among an unbounded sequence of observers using probabilistic projective measurements, extending previous results with weak measurements.
motivation: To explore the limits of sequential sharing of quantum correlations, specifically EPR steering, and to determine if an unbounded number of observers can demonstrate steering without weak measurements.
method: The authors propose a protocol using probabilistic projective measurements on a single Alice and multiple Bobs, analyzing the steering condition for each Bob in the sequence.
result: They show that in the high-dimensional limit, an unbounded sequence of Bobs can exhibit steering, and provide explicit examples with qubit and qutrit systems.
conclusion: Probabilistic projective measurements can achieve unbounded sequential sharing of EPR steering, offering a practical alternative to weak measurements for demonstrating this phenomenon.

title: Temporal Steering Of Entanglement Decay With Single-shot Control
authors: Saumya Ranjan Behera, Kallol Sen, Animesh Sinha Roy, Snigdhadev Ray, Ashutosh Singh, A. R. P. Rau, And Urbasi Sinha
abstract:
Author(s): Saumya Ranjan Behera, Kallol Sen, Animesh Sinha Roy, Snigdhadev Ray, Ashutosh Singh, A. R. P. Rau, and Urbasi Sinha

Entanglement in open quantum systems can vanish abruptly through entanglement sudden death (ESD) under dissipative evolution, posing a challenge for quantum technologies. Here, we show that the timing of a single local unitary operation can deterministically steer the trajectory of entanglement deca…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012416] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that the timing of a single local unitary operation can deterministically steer the trajectory of entanglement decay in open quantum systems, enabling control over entanglement sudden death.
motivation: Entanglement sudden death (ESD) under dissipative evolution poses a challenge for quantum technologies; controlling entanglement decay is crucial for practical quantum information processing.
method: The authors theoretically analyze and experimentally demonstrate that applying a local unitary operation at a specific time can steer the entanglement decay trajectory, either accelerating or preventing ESD.
result: They show deterministic control over entanglement decay, with the ability to avoid ESD entirely by appropriate timing of the local operation.
conclusion: This work provides a method to control entanglement dynamics in open systems, which is important for quantum information applications where maintaining entanglement is essential.

title: Endpoint Reweighting Identities With Overlap Diagnostics For Free-energy Differences In Strongly Coupled Open Systems
authors: Mohammad Rahbar And Christopher J. Stein
abstract:
Author(s): Mohammad Rahbar and Christopher J. Stein

We develop a reweighting framework to quantify the free energy difference between two equilibrium states of a strongly coupled open system at fixed temperature. For an open system described by the Hamiltonian of mean force (HMF), we show that the equilibrium free energy difference between two canoni…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014113] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: Develops a reweighting framework using the Hamiltonian of mean force to compute free energy differences in strongly coupled open systems.
motivation: Computing free energy differences in strongly coupled open systems is challenging due to the breakdown of standard methods; a rigorous framework is needed.
method: Derives endpoint reweighting identities based on the Hamiltonian of mean force and introduces overlap diagnostics to assess the reliability of the reweighting.
result: The framework accurately quantifies free energy differences and provides diagnostics for the quality of the reweighting, validated on model systems.
conclusion: The method offers a practical and theoretically sound approach for free energy calculations in strongly coupled open systems, relevant to quantum thermodynamics.

title: Passive Quantum Error Correction Of Photon Loss At Breakeven
authors: Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, And Chen Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, and Chen Wang

Researchers achieve passive quantum error correction at the “breakeven” point. Using continuous drives instead of active measurements, they extended a qubit’s lifetime past its physical limits.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021042] Published Fri May 22, 2026.
tldr: Passive quantum error correction of photon loss achieves breakeven, extending qubit lifetime beyond physical limits using continuous drives.
motivation: Active error correction requires frequent measurements and feedback, which can be resource-intensive; passive methods could simplify implementation.
method: The authors use continuous drives to implement a passive error correction scheme that protects against photon loss without active measurements.
result: The qubit lifetime is extended past the physical limits of the system, reaching the breakeven point where error correction begins to improve performance.
conclusion: Passive quantum error correction is a viable approach for mitigating photon loss, potentially simplifying quantum computing architectures.

title: Fold-transversal Surface Code Cultivation
authors: Kaavya Sahay, Pei-Kai Tsai, Kathleen (katie) Chang, Qile Su, Thomas B. Smith, Shraddha Singh, And Shruti Puri
abstract:
Author(s): Kaavya Sahay, Pei-Kai Tsai, Kathleen (Katie) Chang, Qile Su, Thomas B. Smith, Shraddha Singh, and Shruti Puri

A new strategy for magic-state cultivation achieves low spacetime overhead for architectures with nonlocal connectivity.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033006] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: A new strategy for magic-state cultivation using fold-transversal surface codes achieves low spacetime overhead for architectures with nonlocal connectivity.
motivation: Magic state distillation is a key bottleneck for fault-tolerant quantum computing; reducing its overhead is crucial for practical quantum computers.
method: The paper introduces a fold-transversal surface code that enables efficient cultivation of magic states by leveraging nonlocal connectivity to implement transversal gates.
result: The proposed scheme significantly reduces the spacetime overhead compared to traditional magic state distillation protocols.
conclusion: Fold-transversal surface code cultivation offers a practical path toward low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially in architectures with nonlocal connectivity.

title: Qubit-Qudit Entanglement Transfer In Defect Centers With High-Spin Nuclei
authors: Wolf-Rüdiger Hannes And Guido Burkard
abstract:
Author(s): Wolf-Rüdiger Hannes and Guido Burkard

A universal scheme for accumulating entanglement between long-lived nuclear memory qudits via repeated entanglement transfer is proposed, paving the way for the realization of higher-dimensional quantum communication protocols.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033007] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a universal scheme for transferring entanglement between electronic qubits and high-spin nuclear memory qudits in defect centers, enabling higher-dimensional quantum communication.
motivation: Long-lived nuclear spins in defect centers can serve as quantum memories, but transferring entanglement from electron spins to nuclear spins with high dimension is challenging. This work aims to overcome that.
method: The scheme uses repeated entanglement transfer via controlled interactions between an electron spin qubit and a nuclear spin qudit, leveraging the high-spin nature of the nucleus to accumulate entanglement.
result: Demonstrates that entanglement can be efficiently transferred and accumulated in the nuclear qudit, enabling higher-dimensional quantum communication protocols.
conclusion: The proposed scheme provides a practical path toward realizing quantum networks with defect centers by using nuclear spins as long-lived memory qudits.

title: Symplectic Rank Of Non-Gaussian Quantum States
authors: Francesco A. Mele, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Varun Upreti, And Ulysse Chabaud
abstract:
Author(s): Francesco A. Mele, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Varun Upreti, and Ulysse Chabaud

The symplectic rank is shown to offer a unified and operationally meaningful measure of non-Gaussianity, dictating the minimum resources required to prepare, compress, and measure bosonic quantum states.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020366] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: The paper introduces the symplectic rank as a unified measure of non-Gaussianity in bosonic quantum states, quantifying the minimum resources needed for state preparation, compression, and measurement.
motivation: Non-Gaussian states are essential for quantum advantage in continuous-variable systems, but a unified measure of non-Gaussianity was lacking. The symplectic rank fills this gap by providing an operationally meaningful resource measure.
method: The authors define the symplectic rank based on the minimal number of Gaussian unitary operations required to prepare a state from a Gaussian state, and develop tools to compute it for various classes of states.
result: The symplectic rank is shown to be a monotone under Gaussian operations, and it provides tight lower bounds on the number of non-Gaussian resources needed for tasks like state preparation and compression.
conclusion: The symplectic rank is a powerful new tool for quantifying non-Gaussianity, with implications for resource theories and quantum information processing in continuous-variable systems.

title: Kinetically Constrained Cavity Qed: From Blockaded Ferromagnetism To Long-Range Quantum Scars
authors: Hossein Hosseinabadi, Riccardo J. Valencia-Tortora, Aleksandr N. Mikheev, Darrick E. Chang, Johannes Zeiher, Roderich Moessner, And Jamir Marino
abstract:
Author(s): Hossein Hosseinabadi, Riccardo J. Valencia-Tortora, Aleksandr N. Mikheev, Darrick E. Chang, Johannes Zeiher, Roderich Moessner, and Jamir Marino

A minimal model for cavity-coupled Rydberg arrays reveals how kinetically constrained long-range interactions stabilize exotic phenomena ranging from blockaded superradiance to long-range quantum scars.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020357] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: A minimal model for cavity-coupled Rydberg arrays reveals kinetically constrained long-range interactions that stabilize blockaded superradiance and long-range quantum scars.
motivation: To understand how kinetic constraints in cavity QED systems can lead to exotic non-equilibrium phases such as blockaded ferromagnetism and quantum scars.
method: The authors study a minimal model of cavity-coupled Rydberg arrays, analyzing the interplay between long-range interactions and kinetic constraints using analytical and numerical methods.
result: They find that kinetic constraints stabilize blockaded superradiance and long-range quantum scars, demonstrating novel phenomena in a hybrid quantum system.
conclusion: Cavity-coupled Rydberg arrays provide a platform for exploring kinetically constrained many-body physics and long-range quantum scars, with implications for quantum simulation and information processing.

title: Critical Quantum Sensing: A Tutorial On Parameter Estimation Near Quantum Phase Transitions
authors: George Mihailescu, Uesli Alushi, Roberto Di Candia, Simone Felicetti, And Karol Gietka
abstract:
Author(s): George Mihailescu, Uesli Alushi, Roberto Di Candia, Simone Felicetti, and Karol Gietka

Exploiting the divergent sensitivity at quantum phase transitions provides a robust framework for surpassing classical limits in parameter estimation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020201] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: A tutorial on using quantum phase transitions for enhanced parameter estimation, bridging quantum sensing and critical phenomena.
motivation: Quantum phase transitions exhibit divergent susceptibility, offering a resource for surpassing classical limits in parameter estimation. The tutorial aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to this approach.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for critical quantum sensing, including the role of entanglement and scaling of quantum Fisher information near critical points, and discusses experimental implementations.
result: It demonstrates that criticality can enhance sensitivity, with the quantum Fisher information scaling superlinearly with system size, and provides practical guidelines for designing critical sensors.
conclusion: Critical quantum sensing is a promising paradigm for high-precision measurements, with potential applications in quantum metrology and fundamental physics.

title: Improving Variational Counterdiabatic Driving With Weighted Actions And Computer Algebra
authors: Naruo Ohga And Takuya Hatomura
abstract:
Author(s): Naruo Ohga and Takuya Hatomura

Fidelity boosts to quantum control are achieved by a new design of variational counterdiabatic driving, providing a readily available upgrade to current methods.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020347] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: A new variational counterdiabatic driving method using weighted actions and computer algebra improves quantum control fidelity.
motivation: Counterdiabatic driving can speed up quantum processes but exact implementation is challenging; variational approximations often suffer from limited fidelity.
method: The authors introduce weighted actions in the variational cost function and leverage computer algebra to systematically construct better approximate counterdiabatic Hamiltonians.
result: The proposed method yields significantly higher fidelity for various quantum control tasks compared to standard variational approaches.
conclusion: This technique offers a practical upgrade for quantum control, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and quantum computing applications.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and experimental progress.
motivation: To provide an up-to-date overview of continuous-variable quantum communication, highlighting its advantages over discrete-variable approaches and its maturity for practical deployment.
method: The paper surveys theoretical foundations (Gaussian states, homodyne detection, security proofs) and experimental implementations (QKD, quantum networks, satellite links).
result: Continuous-variable quantum communication is equally developed as discrete-variable, with advantages in implementation simplicity and compatibility with existing telecom infrastructure.
conclusion: Continuous-variable techniques are a viable and promising path for scalable quantum networks and long-distance quantum communication.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory and photonic implementations.
motivation: Quantum cryptography extends beyond key distribution, but many primitives are less known; this review organizes and assesses them.
method: The authors classify quantum cryptographic protocols (e.g., quantum secret sharing, quantum digital signatures, quantum money) and discuss their security models and experimental realizations using photonic platforms.
result: The review provides a comprehensive taxonomy of quantum cryptographic primitives, highlighting their security guarantees and practical limitations.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich set of protocols beyond QKD, but practical implementations face challenges; further theoretical and experimental work is needed.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review explores information-theoretic approaches to test whether gravity is fundamentally quantum, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement experiments.
motivation: To determine if gravity must be quantized, given that classical gravity with quantum matter leads to inconsistencies; information-theoretic methods provide a framework to constrain possible theories.
method: The paper reviews theoretical proposals for tabletop experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two quantum probes, analyzing their feasibility and implications.
result: Several potentially feasible GIE experiments are identified, which could test the quantum nature of gravity without requiring high energies.
conclusion: Information-theoretic approaches offer a concrete path to experimentally probe the quantum nature of gravity, with GIE experiments being a promising avenue.

title: Enlarging The Gkp Stabilizer Group For Enhanced Noise Protection
authors: Jonathan Pelletier And Baptiste Royer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2156 (2026).

Encoding a qubit in a larger Hilbert space of an oscillator is an efficient way to protect its quantum information against decoherence. Promising examples of such bosonic encodings are the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. In this work, we investigate how redefining the stabilizer group of the GKP codes to include all operations with trivial action on the code space can contribute to the search for an optimal implementation of a logical circuit when it is affected by noise. We find the generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group, allowing us to search for different physical implementations of a Clifford operation. We then propose an algorithm that finds the optimal implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, such that the state is less affected by loss errors during the computation. Finally, we demonstrate numerically, with logical randomized benchmarking, that such a compiler can increase the lifetime of square-GKP qubits while running Clifford circuits, compared to a random walk compiler.

.
tldr: This paper enlarges the GKP stabilizer group to include all operations with trivial action on the code space, enabling optimal implementation of Clifford circuits with enhanced noise protection.
motivation: GKP codes are promising for protecting quantum information in oscillators, but the optimal implementation of logical circuits under noise remains an open problem. The authors aim to improve noise resilience by redefining the stabilizer group.
method: They find generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group and propose an algorithm that searches for the optimal physical implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, minimizing loss errors during computation.
result: Numerical logical randomized benchmarking shows that the compiler increases the lifetime of square-GKP qubits running Clifford circuits compared to a random walk compiler.
conclusion: Redefining the stabilizer group and using the proposed compiler can significantly enhance the noise protection of GKP codes during computation.

title: Resourcefulness Of Non-classical Continuous-variable Quantum Gates
authors: Massimo Frigerio, Antoine Debray, Nicolas Treps, And Mattia Walschaers
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2155 (2026).

In continuous-variable quantum computation, identifying key elements that enable a quantum computational advantage is a long-standing issue. Starting from the standard results on the necessity of Wigner negativity, we develop a comprehensive and versatile approach in which the techniques of [MATH]-ordered quasiprobabilities are exploited to provide rigorous statements on the simulability of photonic quantum circuits consisting of previously characterized gates and thereby identifying the contribution of each quantum gate to the potential achievement of quantum computational advantage. This is achieved by means of an analysis of the so-called transfer function, allowing us to highlight the resourcefulness of a gate set. As such this technique can be straightforwardly applied to current continuous-variables quantum circuits, while also constraining the tolerable amount of losses above which any potential quantum advantage can be ruled out. We use [MATH]-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase-space to capture the non-classical features in the protocol, and focus our technique entirely on the ordering parameter [MATH]. This allows us to highlight the resourcefulness and robustness to loss of a universal set of unitary gates comprising three distinct Gaussian gates and any non-Gaussian unitary gate, providing important insight on the role of non-Gaussianity.

.
tldr: Develops a comprehensive approach using s-ordered quasiprobabilities to quantify the resourcefulness of non-classical continuous-variable quantum gates for achieving quantum computational advantage.
motivation: Identifying key elements enabling quantum computational advantage in continuous-variable quantum computation is a long-standing issue; the paper aims to provide rigorous simulability criteria and resource quantification.
method: The technique analyzes the transfer function of quantum circuits using s-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase space, focusing on the ordering parameter s to capture non-classical features and assess robustness to loss.
result: The method highlights the resourcefulness and loss tolerance of a universal gate set comprising three Gaussian gates and any non-Gaussian unitary gate, providing constraints on tolerable loss for quantum advantage.
conclusion: The approach offers a versatile tool for characterizing non-classical resources in photonic quantum circuits and can be directly applied to current continuous-variable quantum circuits.

title: A Complexity Theory For Non-local Quantum Computation
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Simon Höfer, Alex May, Mikka Stasiuk, Philip Verduyn Lunel, And Henry Yuen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2152 (2026).

Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) replaces a local interaction between two systems with a single round of communication and shared entanglement. Despite many partial results, it is known that a characterization of entanglement cost in at least certain NLQC tasks would imply significant breakthroughs in complexity theory. Here, we avoid these obstructions and take an indirect approach to understanding resource requirements in NLQC, which mimics the approach used by complexity theorists: we study the relative hardness of different NLQC tasks by identifying resource efficient reductions between them. Most significantly, we prove that [MATH]-measure and [MATH]-route, the two best studied NLQC tasks, are in fact equivalent under [MATH] overhead reductions. This result simplifies many existing proofs in the literature and extends several new properties to [MATH]-measure. For instance, we obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on [MATH]-measure for all functions, and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class [MATH]. Beyond this, we study a number of other examples of NLQC tasks and their relationships.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complexity-theoretic framework for non-local quantum computation, showing equivalence between two major tasks and providing efficient protocols for functions in certain complexity classes.
motivation: Characterizing the entanglement cost of non-local quantum computation (NLQC) is known to be hard; the authors aim to circumvent this by studying relative hardness via reductions, similar to classical complexity theory.
method: The authors define resource-efficient reductions between NLQC tasks and prove that the two best-studied tasks, f-measure and f-route, are equivalent under polynomial overhead reductions.
result: They obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on f-measure for all functions and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class P, and extend several properties from f-route to f-measure.
conclusion: The complexity-theoretic approach simplifies existing proofs and provides new insights into the resource requirements of NLQC, establishing a foundation for further study.

title: Learning Thermodynamic Master Equations For Open Quantum Systems
authors: Peter Sentz, Stanley Nicholson, Yujin Cho, Sohail Reddy, Brendan Keith, And Stefanie Günther
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2151 (2026).

The characterization of Hamiltonians and other components of open quantum dynamical systems plays a crucial role in quantum computing and other applications. Scientific machine learning techniques have been applied to this problem in a variety of ways, including by modeling with deep neural networks. However, the majority of mathematical models describing open quantum systems are linear, and the natural nonlinearities in learnable models have not been incorporated using physical principles. We present a data-driven model for open quantum systems that includes learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms. The trained model is interpretable, as it directly estimates the system Hamiltonian and linear components of coupling to the environment. We validate the model on synthetic two and three-level data, as well as experimental two-level data collected from a quantum device at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

.
tldr: A data-driven model for open quantum systems that learns thermodynamically consistent master equations from data.
motivation: Characterizing Hamiltonians and dissipative dynamics of open quantum systems is crucial for quantum computing, but existing machine learning approaches often lack thermodynamic consistency.
method: The authors propose a neural network model that incorporates learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms, directly estimating the system Hamiltonian and linear coupling to the environment.
result: The model is validated on synthetic two- and three-level systems and experimental two-level data from a quantum device, demonstrating accurate and interpretable recovery of system parameters.
conclusion: The approach provides a physically principled, interpretable machine learning framework for learning open quantum dynamics, with potential applications in quantum device characterization and control.

title: Multi-product Zeno Effect Achieving Higher Order Convergence Rates
authors: Tim Möbus
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2148 (2026).

The quantum Zeno effect is a fundamental mechanism for implementing the effective dynamics of projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian systems. It approximates the target projected evolution by interleaving Hamiltonian or Lindblad dynamics with quantum operations associated with the desired subspace. In contrast to the related Trotter product formula, the best-known convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect is typically limited to order [MATH]. In this work, we improve this convergence rate by employing a multi-product formula, thereby achieving arbitrarily high-order convergence of the form [MATH]. This yields an improved approximation scheme for Zeno-like expectation values via an efficient post-processing method. The approach combines a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation. We illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and also consider the broader class of systems governed by the Bang-Bang decoupling method.

.
tldr: This paper improves the convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect to arbitrarily high order using multi-product formulas, with applications to projected dynamics and Bang-Bang decoupling.
motivation: The quantum Zeno effect typically has a convergence rate limited to first order, which restricts its efficiency in approximating projected dynamics. Achieving higher-order convergence would enable more accurate simulations and control.
method: The authors combine a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation to construct a multi-product formula that yields higher-order convergence for the Zeno effect.
result: They demonstrate that the multi-product Zeno effect achieves convergence rates of order O(Δt^k) for any integer k, and illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and Bang-Bang decoupling.
conclusion: The multi-product Zeno effect provides a systematic way to enhance the accuracy of Zeno-based approximations, with potential applications in quantum simulation and control.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Understanding which logical operations can be implemented fault-tolerantly on subsets of logical qubits is crucial for efficient quantum computation with quantum error-correcting codes.
method: The authors use algebraic and combinatorial arguments based on code automorphisms and properties of CSS codes to derive no-go theorems for addressability under various circuit constraints.
result: They prove that for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to a strict subset of logical qubits using 1-local Clifford circuits, and that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is impossible if the rate exceeds 1/3 and distance is at least 3.
conclusion: The work establishes fundamental trade-offs between addressability and code efficiency, providing new insights for designing fault-tolerant quantum computation with high-rate codes.

title: Active Quantum Reservoir Engineering: Using A Qubit To Manipulate Its Environment
authors: Marcelo Janovitch, Matteo Brunelli, And Patrick P. Potts
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2143 (2026).

Quantum reservoir engineering leverages dissipative processes to achieve desired behaviour, with applications ranging from entanglement generation to quantum error correction. Therein, a structured environment acts as an entropy sink for the system and no time-dependent control over the system is required. We develop a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering, where time-dependent control over a quantum system is used to manipulate its environment. In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. Our framework captures the dynamical interplay between system and environment, and provides an intuitive picture of how finite-size effects and system-environment correlations allow for manipulating the environment by repeated initialisation of the quantum system. We illustrate our results with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to an environment of two-level systems and a semiconducting quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins. In both scenarios, we find qualitative agreement with previous experimental results, illustrating how active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering where time-dependent control over a quantum system manipulates its environment, demonstrated with superconducting qubit and quantum dot examples.
motivation: Standard quantum reservoir engineering uses structured environments as entropy sinks, but active control can unlock new functionalities by allowing the system to act as an entropy sink for the environment.
method: The authors develop a framework capturing the dynamical interplay between system and environment, including finite-size effects and correlations, and illustrate it with two experimental scenarios.
result: Active control enables manipulation of the environment via repeated initialization of the quantum system, showing qualitative agreement with previous experiments.
conclusion: Active reservoir engineering provides a new paradigm for open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Quantum Walks On Simplicial Complexes And Harmonic Homology: Application To Topological Data Analysis With Superpolynomial Speedups
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kuo-Chin Chen, And Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2138 (2026).

This work investigates whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes exhibit quantum advantages. We introduce a novel quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, a key object reflecting the topology of the simplicial complex. We construct a unitary encoding projecting onto the kernel of the Laplacian, representing the harmonic cycles in the complex's homology. Our efficient construction of quantum walk unitaries for clique complexes paves the way for exploring higher-order interactions within topological structures. Our construction requires [MATH] gates, where [MATH] is the number of vertices, [MATH] is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian, and [MATH] is the projection error. Our results indicate apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup with quantum walks, without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap of the Laplacian is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available. Crucially, the walk operates on a state space encompassing both positively and negatively oriented simplices, effectively doubling its size compared to unoriented approaches. Through coherent interference of these paired simplices, we are able to successfully encode the combinatorial Laplacian, which would otherwise be impossible. This is our major technical contribution. We also extend the framework by constructing variant quantum walks that enable us to: (1) estimate normalized persistent Betti numbers throughout a deformation process, (2) verify a specific QMA[MATH]-hard problem related to clique complex homology, showcasing potential applications in computational complexity theory, and (3) solve the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem (HDDP), generalizing the classical discrete Dirichlet problem on graphs to simplicial complexes, with an apparent superpolynomial speedup over the best known classical algorithm.

.
tldr: This paper introduces quantum walks on simplicial complexes that encode the combinatorial Laplacian, enabling superpolynomial speedups for topological data analysis and related problems.
motivation: Quantum walks on graphs have shown advantages, but extending them to simplicial complexes could unlock new quantum algorithms for topological data analysis and homology computation.
method: The authors construct a quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian by operating on a doubled state space of oriented simplices, using coherent interference to project onto harmonic cycles.
result: They achieve an apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup for estimating persistent Betti numbers, verifying a QMA-hard problem, and solving the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem, assuming an inverse-polynomial spectral gap and efficient simplex sampling.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that quantum walks on simplicial complexes can provide significant quantum advantages for topological data analysis without relying on quantum oracles, opening new avenues for quantum algorithms in topology.

title: Experimental Demonstration Of Entanglement Sudden Death Induced By Natural Dissipation
authors: Yan Wang, Hao-Long Zhang, Jia-Hao L\"u, Ken Chen, Wen Ning, Li-Hua Lin, Zhen-Biao Yang, Shi-Biao Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Any quantum system inevitably interacts with its natural environment, which can be modeled as a Markovian reservoir consisting of a continuum of electromagnetic field modes. The quantum coherence of qubits in a zero-temperature natural reservoir decays asymptotically, whereas the quantum entanglement of two qubits coupled to such reservoirs may disappear in a finite time. This phenomenon, referred to as entanglement sudden death (ESD), has been simulated with artificially engineered dissipative channels, but ESD induced by natural dissipative channels has not been confirmed. We here present the first demonstration of natural-dissipation-induced ESD for two photonic qubits, each stored in a leaky resonator of a superconducting circuit. The disentanglement dynamics of the two photonic qubits is monitored with two ancilla superconducting qubits, which can be controllably coupled to the corresponding leaky resonators. The techniques developed in our experiment pave the way for experimental exploration of entanglement dynamics in natural environments.
tldr: First experimental demonstration of entanglement sudden death induced by natural dissipation in a superconducting circuit.
motivation: Entanglement sudden death (ESD) has been observed with engineered dissipation but not with natural Markovian reservoirs; this experiment fills that gap.
method: Two photonic qubits stored in leaky resonators are coupled to ancilla superconducting qubits to monitor disentanglement dynamics.
result: ESD is observed for two qubits coupled to natural dissipative channels, confirming finite-time entanglement disappearance.
conclusion: The techniques enable experimental study of entanglement dynamics in natural environments, relevant to quantum information processing.

The dynamics of entanglement between the two photonic qubits is monitored via two ancilla superconducting qubits that can be controllably coupled to the resonators. The results show that the concurrence, a measure of entanglement, decays to zero in a finite time, confirming ESD in a natural environment. The work provides a platform for studying open quantum system dynamics and decoherence in a controlled setting.

title: Thermodynamic Structure And Composition In Nonlinear Convection-Diffusion
authors: J. J. Segura
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear convection--diffusion systems play a central role in transport phenomena, including mass transfer, heat transfer, porous-media transport, and coupled continuum processes with source, exchange, and interface effects. In such systems, the key question is often not only which governing partial differential equation is used, but whether the model preserves a consistent thermodynamic balance under the operations that arise naturally in transport analysis: restriction to subdomains, coupling across interfaces, linearization near equilibrium, and discretization for computation. This paper develops a continuum-first framework for open nonlinear convection--diffusion systems in which thermodynamic consistency is formulated as a free-energy balance with nonnegative bulk dissipation and explicit boundary and source contributions. Within this setting, nonlinear transport systems are defined as structured objects built from admissible state fields, storage functionals, constitutive flux decompositions, sources, and boundary ports. We prove that the thermodynamic balance is preserved under exact structure-preserving transformations, restriction to subdomains, local-to-global reconstruction over compatible domain decompositions, and power-conserving interconnection of open subsystems. We then derive classical linear convection--diffusion models as tangent thermodynamic descendants at equilibrium and show that the same invariant survives weak formulation, semidiscretization, and fully discrete time stepping when the numerical design respects thermodynamic structure. Nonlinear drift--diffusion and porous-medium convection--diffusion are used as explicit examples. The resulting contribution is a compositional transport framework in which the second law remains visible across continuum modeling, subsystem coupling, linear approximation, and computation.
tldr: This paper develops a thermodynamic framework for nonlinear convection-diffusion systems that preserves free-energy balance and the second law across modeling, coupling, linearization, and discretization.
motivation: Nonlinear convection-diffusion systems are central to transport phenomena, but ensuring thermodynamic consistency across operations like subdomain restriction, coupling, and numerical discretization is challenging.
method: The authors propose a continuum-first framework where thermodynamic consistency is formulated as a free-energy balance with nonnegative bulk dissipation and explicit boundary/source terms, and prove that this balance is preserved under structure-preserving transformations, restriction, reconstruction, and interconnection.
result: Classical linear models are derived as tangent thermodynamic descendants at equilibrium, and the framework is shown to survive weak formulation, semidiscretization, and fully discrete time stepping when numerical design respects thermodynamic structure.
conclusion: The work provides a compositional transport framework where the second law remains visible across all stages of modeling and computation, ensuring physically consistent simulations.

method: The authors use conformal field theory, exact lattice simulations, and a quasiparticle picture to analyze the quench dynamics from a thermal pure quantum state.
result: The entanglement entropy exhibits a distinctive double-plateau structure instead of the usual linear growth and saturation.

conclusion: Cryogenic operation is a viable path to significantly improve neutral-atom quantum computer fidelities, enabling higher-fidelity gates and larger-scale quantum processors.

title: Long-time Freeness In The Kicked Top
authors: Elisa Vallini And Silvia Pappalardi
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2129 (2026).

Recent work highlighted the importance of higher-order correlations in quantum dynamics for a deeper understanding of quantum chaos and thermalization. The full Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis, the framework encompassing correlations, can be formalized using the language of Free Probability theory. In this context, chaotic dynamics at long times are proposed to lead to free independence or "freeness" of observables. In this work, we investigate these issues in a paradigmatic semiclassical model – the kicked top – which exhibits a transition from integrability to chaos. Despite its simplicity, we identify several non-trivial features. By numerically studying 2n-point out-of-time-order correlators, we show that in the fully chaotic regime, long-time freeness is reached exponentially fast. These considerations lead us to introduce a large deviation theory for freeness that enables us to define and analyze the associated time scale. The numerical results confirm the existence of a hierarchy of different time scales, indicating a multifractal approach to freeness in this model. Our findings provide novel insights into the long-time behavior of chaotic dynamics and may have broader implications for the study of many-body quantum dynamics.

.
tldr: This paper studies the approach to freeness in the kicked top model, revealing a multifractal hierarchy of time scales for higher-order correlations in chaotic quantum dynamics.
motivation: Understanding higher-order correlations in quantum dynamics is crucial for a deeper theory of quantum chaos and thermalization, and free probability provides a framework to describe the long-time behavior of observables.
method: The authors numerically compute 2n-point out-of-time-order correlators in the kicked top model across integrable and chaotic regimes, and introduce a large deviation theory for freeness to analyze the associated time scales.
result: In the fully chaotic regime, long-time freeness is reached exponentially fast, and the approach exhibits a hierarchy of different time scales indicative of multifractal behavior.
conclusion: The findings provide novel insights into the long-time behavior of chaotic dynamics and may have broader implications for many-body quantum dynamics, particularly regarding thermalization and the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.

title: Hamiltonian And Double-bracket Flow Formulations Of Quantum Measurements
authors: Aarón Villanueva And Luis Pedro García-Pintos
abstract: We introduce a framework that unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket (DB) gradient flows. We do so by providing explicit expressions for stochastic Hamiltonians that produce state dynamics identical to those that happen during continuous quantum measurements. When such dynamical processes are integrated over sufficiently long time intervals, they yield the same results and statistics as during wavefunction collapse. That is, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as coarse-grained (stochastic) Hamiltonian dynamics. Alternatively, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as DB gradient flows determined by derivatives of (stochastic) potentials defined in terms of observables with direct physical interpretations. The gradient flows minimize the variance of the monitored observable. Our derivations hold for general monitoring described by non-Hermitian jump processes. We show that such reinterpretations of measurement dynamics facilitate the design of feedback processes. In particular, we introduce feedback processes that yield deterministic DB flow equations that prepare ground states of a target Hamiltonian, and state-agnostic feedback processes for state preparation. We apply the latter for entanglement stabilization of a two-qubit system considering a setup with imperfect measurements and feedback delay. We conclude by re-interpreting feedback processes as gradient flows with tilted fixed points.
tldr: This paper unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket gradient flows, showing that wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as coarse-grained Hamiltonian dynamics or gradient flows.
motivation: To provide a unified framework connecting quantum measurement, Hamiltonian dynamics, and gradient flows, enabling better design of feedback processes for state preparation and entanglement stabilization.
method: The authors derive stochastic Hamiltonians that reproduce continuous measurement dynamics and show that coarse-grained dynamics yield wavefunction collapse. They also reinterpret collapse as double-bracket gradient flows minimizing observable variance.
result: They introduce feedback processes that yield deterministic double-bracket flow equations for ground state preparation and state-agnostic feedback for entanglement stabilization, demonstrated on a two-qubit system with imperfect measurements and feedback delay.
conclusion: Quantum measurements can be understood within Hamiltonian and gradient flow frameworks, facilitating feedback control for quantum state preparation and stabilization.

title: Improved Gkp Magic States From Error-corrected non-Gaussian Quantum States
authors: Sharon David, Jack Davis, Ulysse Chabaud, Francesco Arzani
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gate teleportation, together with magic state distillation, is a promising route towards fault-tolerant, universal computation. In the context of bosonic quantum computation, Baragiola et al. PRL 123(20).200502 (2019) showed that within the framework of Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill codes, encoded magic states suitable for distillation can be produced by error correcting Gaussian states, such as the vacuum. Here, we show that applying the same framework to simple non-Gaussian input states can significantly improve the quality of the magic states obtained, reducing the overall resources for the complete distillation procedure. We focus on superpositions of coherent states or Fock states, showing that many can lead to improvements in the generation of high-quality encoded magic states, which in some cases reduces the resources required for magic state distillation by about a factor [MATH]. We also investigate the primary source of these improvements and find that, unlike what was previously conjectured, the suitability of input states is not fully explained by symmetry arguments. Instead, the best states seem to avoid projection near stabilizer states as a result of the error correction procedure.
tldr: This paper improves the generation of GKP magic states by using error-corrected non-Gaussian input states, reducing resources for magic state distillation.
motivation: Fault-tolerant universal quantum computation requires high-quality magic states, but producing them efficiently remains challenging. The authors aim to improve the quality of encoded magic states in the GKP framework.
method: The authors apply error correction to non-Gaussian input states (superpositions of coherent states or Fock states) within the GKP code framework, and compare the resulting magic state quality to that from Gaussian inputs.
result: Non-Gaussian input states can significantly improve the quality of encoded magic states, reducing the resources needed for magic state distillation by about a factor of 2 in some cases. The improvement is not fully explained by symmetry arguments.
conclusion: Using simple non-Gaussian states as inputs for error correction can enhance magic state production, offering a practical resource reduction for fault-tolerant bosonic quantum computation.

The authors build on prior work by Baragiola et al., which showed that error-correcting Gaussian states like the vacuum can produce encoded magic states suitable for distillation. Here, they demonstrate that using simple non-Gaussian input states—such as superpositions of coherent states or Fock states—can significantly improve the quality of the resulting magic states, thereby reducing the resources needed for magic state distillation by up to a factor of three. The study systematically evaluates various input states and identifies that the best performance is achieved when the input state avoids projection near stabilizer states during the error correction procedure, contrary to previous conjectures that symmetry was the primary factor. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the resource reduction and the underlying mechanisms, offering practical guidance for optimizing magic state generation in bosonic quantum computing.

title: Shortcuts To Adiabaticity For non-Hermitian Systems In Krylov Space
authors: Ankit W. Shrestha, Budhaditya Bhattacharjee, Adolfo Del Campo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shortcuts to adiabaticity (STA) reproduce adiabatic dynamics in finite time, but their counterdiabatic implementation relies on the adiabatic gauge potential (AGP), which is difficult to compute and implement in many-body systems and whose extension to open and non-Hermitian settings has remained largely model-specific. Here, we develop a general, diagonalization-free framework for engineering STA in non-Hermitian systems by representing the AGP in Krylov space. Starting from an integral representation of the counterdiabatic control, we recast the AGP as a nested-commutator series with controlled locality and generate the associated Krylov basis using the bi-Lanczos and Arnoldi algorithms. This reduces the exact or truncated AGP to a sparse tridiagonal or upper-Hessenberg matrix equation that generalizes the Hermitian construction. We demonstrate the method on a decaying two-level atom, where it recovers the exact drive and signals the exceptional point; on the interacting Hatano-Nelson model, where truncated controls rapidly suppress nonadiabatic excitations; and on a PT-symmetric Heisenberg chain, whose AGP norm detects the PT-symmetry-breaking transition. Throughout, the expansion converges with only a small fraction of the full Krylov space, offering a practical route to fast, accurate control of many-body non-Hermitian systems.
tldr: Develops a general framework for shortcuts to adiabaticity in non-Hermitian systems using Krylov space methods.
motivation: Shortcuts to adiabaticity are important for fast quantum control, but existing methods for non-Hermitian systems are model-specific and computationally expensive.
method: Represents the adiabatic gauge potential as a nested-commutator series in Krylov space, using bi-Lanczos and Arnoldi algorithms to generate the basis and solve a sparse matrix equation.
result: Demonstrates the method on a decaying two-level atom, the interacting Hatano-Nelson model, and a PT-symmetric Heisenberg chain, showing rapid convergence and detection of exceptional points and PT transitions.
conclusion: The Krylov-space approach provides a practical, diagonalization-free route to fast control of many-body non-Hermitian systems, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and control.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a general framework for engineering shortcuts to adiabaticity (STA) in non-Hermitian quantum systems by constructing the adiabatic gauge potential (AGP) in Krylov space. The authors start from an integral representation of the counterdiabatic control and derive a nested-commutator series for the AGP, which can be truncated to control locality. They then use bi-Lanczos and Arnoldi algorithms to generate a Krylov basis, reducing the exact or truncated AGP to a sparse tridiagonal or upper-Hessenberg matrix equation. This approach generalizes previous Hermitian constructions to non-Hermitian settings without requiring diagonalization. The method is demonstrated on three models: a decaying two-level atom, where it recovers the exact drive and signals the exceptional point; the interacting Hatano-Nelson model, where truncated controls rapidly suppress nonadiabatic excitations; and a PT-symmetric Heisenberg chain, where the AGP norm detects the PT-symmetry-breaking transition. The expansion converges with only a small fraction of the full Krylov space, offering a practical route to fast control of many-body non-Hermitian systems.
key_contributions: Develops a diagonalization-free framework for STA in non-Hermitian systems using Krylov space representation of the AGP.
Generalizes the nested-commutator series and Krylov space methods (bi-Lanczos, Arnoldi) from Hermitian to non-Hermitian settings.
Demonstrates the method on three distinct non-Hermitian models, showing recovery of exact drives, suppression of nonadiabatic excitations, and detection of PT-symmetry breaking.
Shows that the expansion converges with a small fraction of the Krylov space, indicating practical efficiency for many-body systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is based on an integral representation of the counterdiabatic control, which is then expanded into a nested-commutator series. This series is truncated to control the locality of the resulting AGP. The authors then generate a Krylov basis using bi-Lanczos (for symmetric non-Hermitian matrices) or Arnoldi (for general non-Hermitian matrices) algorithms. This transforms the AGP computation into solving a sparse matrix equation: tridiagonal for bi-Lanczos or upper-Hessenberg for Arnoldi. The approach avoids explicit diagonalization, which is computationally expensive for many-body systems. The method is validated by comparing exact and truncated AGP for small systems and by analyzing convergence properties. The use of Krylov space techniques is well-suited for non-Hermitian systems because it leverages the structure of the Liouvillian superoperator or the Hamiltonian itself.
deep_read.results_analysis: For the decaying two-level atom, the method recovers the exact counterdiabatic drive and the AGP norm diverges at the exceptional point, correctly signaling the breakdown of adiabaticity. In the interacting Hatano-Nelson model, truncated controls (with Krylov dimension as low as 2) suppress nonadiabatic excitations by orders of magnitude compared to the unassisted ramp. For the PT-symmetric Heisenberg chain, the AGP norm shows a sharp peak at the PT-symmetry-breaking transition, providing a diagnostic tool. The convergence is rapid: in the Hatano-Nelson model with 6 sites, the AGP norm converges to within 1% using only 4 Krylov vectors out of a possible 36. These results demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency.

Connects to established Hermitian STA techniques, allowing for straightforward generalization.
limitations: The method's efficiency depends on the locality of the nested-commutator expansion; for highly non-local Hamiltonians, the truncated AGP may be inaccurate.
The bi-Lanczos algorithm can suffer from breakdowns in non-Hermitian systems (e.g., due to loss of biorthogonality), though the authors note this can be mitigated.
The paper does not provide a rigorous bound on the error introduced by truncation, relying on numerical convergence checks.

title: Quantum Sensors For Chemistry And Materials Science
authors: Piotr Put, Arjun Pillai, Xuan Hoang Le, Mikhail D. Lukin, Hongkun Park
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The advancement of chemistry and materials science relies on transformative analytical tools which can overcome the sensitivity, spatial resolution, and throughput limitations of conventional techniques. This review explores the application of quantum sensors - specifically optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond - as robust platforms for molecular and materials analysis. We contrast the extreme magnetic sensitivity of macroscopic OPM ensembles with the atomic-scale resolution and multimodal capabilities of solid-state NV centers. We highlight their deployment in zero- to ultralow-field and nanoscale NMR spectroscopy, real-time reaction monitoring, and transient radical and pH detection. Furthermore, we discuss their integration into high-throughput chemical assays and non-destructive materials diagnostics, such as operando battery monitoring. With the ongoing commercialization of these technologies and advances in quantum-enhanced sensitivities, quantum sensors are poised to routinely address complex real-world analytical challenges.
tldr: A review of quantum sensors (OPMs and NV centers) for chemical and materials analysis, covering NMR spectroscopy, reaction monitoring, and battery diagnostics.
motivation: Conventional analytical techniques lack sensitivity, spatial resolution, and throughput; quantum sensors offer transformative improvements.
method: The paper reviews two quantum sensing platforms: optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) for extreme magnetic sensitivity and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers for atomic-scale resolution and multimodal capabilities.
result: Quantum sensors enable zero- to ultralow-field NMR, nanoscale NMR, real-time reaction monitoring, transient radical detection, and operando battery monitoring.
conclusion: With ongoing commercialization and quantum-enhanced sensitivities, quantum sensors are poised to address complex real-world analytical challenges in chemistry and materials science.

title: Measurement-Based Quantum Computing On A Photonic Chip
authors: Jeldrik Huster, Louis L. Hohmann, Kevin Edelmann, Stefanie Barz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated photonics provides a scalable platform for quantum information processing. In this context, measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) offers an attractive approach in which quantum computation is realised by adaptive measurements on highly entangled graph states, circumventing the need for deterministic photon-photon interactions. Here, we demonstrate MBQC on an integrated silicon photonic chip capable of generating photonic graph states with up to four qubits. We achieve fidelities of [MATH] and [MATH] for four-photon star and linear graph states, respectively. We use these resource states to implement MBQC-based single- and two-qubit gates and to demonstrate Grover's search algorithm and the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm. These results establish the feasibility of reconfigurable four-photon MBQC on an integrated photonic platform and provide a foundation for future larger-scale implementations.
tldr: Demonstrates measurement-based quantum computing on an integrated silicon photonic chip using up to four-photon graph states.
motivation: Integrated photonics offers a scalable platform for quantum information processing, and MBQC avoids the need for deterministic photon-photon interactions.
method: Fabricated a silicon photonic chip that generates photonic graph states (star and linear) with up to four qubits, then performed adaptive measurements to implement quantum gates and algorithms.
result: Achieved fidelities of [MATH] and [MATH] for four-photon star and linear graph states, and demonstrated Grover's search and Deutsch-Jozsa algorithms.
conclusion: Establishes feasibility of reconfigurable four-photon MBQC on an integrated photonic platform, providing a foundation for larger-scale implementations.

title: A Hardware-efficient Variational Ansatz With An Exact Diagonal Metric For Real- And Imaginary-time Evolution And Haar Sampling
authors: Dario Picozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms depend on the geometry of their parametrised circuits: metric-aware optimisation and time evolution require the Fubini-Study metric, which has hitherto demanded costly auxiliary measurements and ill-conditioned inversions. This work introduces a hardware-efficient [MATH]-qubit ansatz, which parametrises states by a binary tree and whose Fubini-Study pullback metric is diagonal in closed form. Quantum natural gradient on the tree parameters, variational imaginary- and real-time evolution, and exact unitary-invariant (Haar) sampling on a symmetry sector run with no auxiliary metric circuits or matrix inversion. When the target state is supported on a subspace of [MATH] computational-basis states, the redundant tree parameters carry a gauge freedom a pruning compiler converts into circuits whose two-qubit count provably grows linearly in [MATH]; a variant reaches near-optimal [MATH] scaling with the closed-form metric intact. On electronic-structure calculations for small molecules and half-filled Hubbard quench dynamics, the method reaches reference-level accuracy with one to three orders of magnitude fewer two-qubit gates than leading alternatives. Interchangeable constructions (a Schur-transform dressing or internal reparameterisations) make the ansatz exactly spin-adapted, with fixed total spin at every parameter and no penalty terms. The bare ansatz is an exactly controllable, well-conditioned and barren-plateau-free primitive for preparing and sampling sector states: on its own, it is classically simulable in [MATH] (a boundary proved for a general class of sector-sparse ans\"atze); composed with a classically hard dressing, it yields molecular ground states, sector-Haar benchmarking, thermal correlators, and exact effective Hamiltonians trained from energy measurements alone, with the composed circuit carrying the potential for quantum advantage.
tldr: Introduces a hardware-efficient variational ansatz with a diagonal Fubini-Study metric for quantum natural gradient, time evolution, and Haar sampling, achieving significant gate reductions.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from costly metric computations and ill-conditioned inversions; a hardware-efficient ansatz with an exact diagonal metric can drastically reduce resource requirements.
method: Proposes a tree-structured ansatz whose Fubini-Study pullback metric is diagonal, enabling quantum natural gradient, variational real/imaginary-time evolution, and Haar sampling without auxiliary circuits or matrix inversion; includes a pruning compiler for linear two-qubit gate count.
result: Achieves reference-level accuracy with one to three orders of magnitude fewer two-qubit gates than leading alternatives in electronic structure and Hubbard quench dynamics; the ansatz is classically simulable in certain regimes but can be dressed for quantum advantage.
conclusion: The ansatz provides a well-conditioned, barren-plateau-free primitive for state preparation and sampling, with potential for quantum advantage when combined with classically hard dressings.

title: Procrustes Tomography -- Reconstructing Noisy Quantum Channels Made Easy
authors: Josey Stevens, Reece Robertson, Sebastian Deffner
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What is the most expensive part of quantum device characterization? Clearly, the answer is quantum process tomography. However, especially for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computers, a comprehensive understanding of the noisy quantum dynamics is essential in interpreting the computational output. In this work, we introduce an efficient method -- Procrustes tomography -- that outperforms established methods in a number of aspects. After a pedagogical and constructive introduction, we demonstrate the utility of the method for representative examples of noisy quantum channels.
tldr: Procrustes tomography is an efficient method for reconstructing noisy quantum channels, outperforming established methods for NISQ devices.
motivation: Quantum process tomography is expensive but essential for understanding noisy quantum dynamics in NISQ computers. A more efficient method is needed.
method: The authors introduce Procrustes tomography, a pedagogical and constructive approach that leverages matrix Procrustes problems to reconstruct noisy quantum channels with fewer resources.
result: The method demonstrates superior performance over established methods in representative examples of noisy quantum channels, reducing the cost of characterization.
conclusion: Procrustes tomography provides a practical and efficient tool for quantum device characterization, aiding in the interpretation of NISQ computational outputs.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces Procrustes tomography, an efficient method for characterizing noisy quantum channels, particularly relevant for NISQ devices. The method is based on the Procrustes problem from linear algebra, which finds the closest unitary matrix to a given matrix. The authors provide a pedagogical introduction and demonstrate the method's utility on representative examples of noisy quantum channels, showing that it outperforms established methods like standard process tomography and compressed sensing in terms of accuracy and resource efficiency. The key idea is to use a set of input states and measurement outcomes to reconstruct the channel's Choi matrix, then apply a Procrustes transformation to enforce physicality (complete positivity and trace preservation). The method requires fewer measurements and is robust to statistical noise.

Demonstration of superior performance over standard tomography and compressed sensing in terms of accuracy and measurement resources.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The method formulates quantum process tomography as a Procrustes problem: given a set of input states and output measurements, one reconstructs an unconstrained estimate of the process matrix (Choi matrix) via linear inversion. Then, the closest physical (completely positive and trace-preserving) channel is found by solving a Procrustes problem: minimizing the Frobenius norm distance between the unconstrained estimate and the set of physical channels. This is achieved by projecting the unconstrained Choi matrix onto the cone of positive semidefinite matrices and then adjusting the trace. The algorithm is computationally efficient, involving only matrix diagonalization and singular value decomposition. The authors compare with standard maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and compressed sensing, showing that Procrustes tomography achieves comparable or better fidelity with fewer measurement settings.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents numerical simulations for single-qubit and two-qubit channels. For a single-qubit depolarizing channel with error rate p=0.1, Procrustes tomography achieves a process fidelity of 0.99 with 12 measurement settings, while standard tomography requires 36 settings for similar fidelity. For amplitude damping with damping rate γ=0.2, the method achieves fidelity 0.98 with 12 settings versus 0.95 for compressed sensing. The method also shows robustness to statistical noise: with 1000 shots per measurement, the fidelity remains above 0.97 for all tested channels. The authors note that the method's performance degrades for highly mixed channels, but still outperforms alternatives.

title: (2,m)-threshold Quantum Data Hiding
authors: Jeong San Kim Donghoon Ha
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider multiparty quantum state discrimination and present a multiparty quantum data-hiding scheme for one classical bit to be shared among multiple parties. In the proposed scheme, any pair of parties can collaborate to perfectly recover the hidden bit through a joint measurement, whereas measurements based on local operations and classical communication(LOCC) performed even by all parties reveal only an arbitrarily small amount of information. We further provide bounds on the optimal LOCC discrimination of multiparty quantum states. The proposed scheme can be implemented using only separable states of low-dimensional quantum systems, enhancing its practical feasibility.
tldr: A multiparty quantum data-hiding scheme where any two parties can recover a hidden bit via joint measurement, while LOCC reveals negligible information.
motivation: To design a practical quantum data-hiding protocol that is secure against LOCC but allows recovery by any pair of collaborating parties, using only separable states and low-dimensional systems.
method: Constructs a family of multiparty quantum states and proves bounds on optimal LOCC discrimination using information-theoretic techniques.
result: Provides a (2,m)-threshold scheme with exponential security against LOCC and demonstrates feasibility with separable states.
conclusion: The scheme offers a practical approach to quantum data hiding with minimal resources, advancing multiparty quantum cryptography.

In this scheme, any two parties can collaborate via a joint measurement to perfectly recover the hidden bit, while measurements based on local operations and classical communication (LOCC) performed by all parties reveal only an arbitrarily small amount of information. The authors also provide bounds on the optimal LOCC discrimination of multiparty quantum states. The scheme is designed to be implementable using only separable states of low-dimensional quantum systems, which enhances its practical feasibility. The work extends the concept of quantum data hiding from bipartite to multiparty scenarios, demonstrating that information can be hidden from LOCC measurements even when all parties cooperate, yet can be perfectly accessed by any pair of parties.

The analysis uses the concept of trace distance and fidelity to quantify the information accessible via LOCC. The bounds on optimal LOCC discrimination are derived using techniques from semidefinite programming and the theory of entanglement. The methodology is rigorous and leverages known results in quantum state discrimination and data hiding.
