title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A review of exactly solvable quantum many-body dynamics using space-time duality and brickwork quantum circuits.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; space-time duality offers a unified approach.
method: The review explains how discretizing time evolution on a lattice and treating space and time symmetrically leads to solvable models via brickwork quantum circuits.
result: The paper provides a pedagogical overview of the relationship between space-time duality and integrable quantum circuits.
conclusion: Space-time duality is a powerful tool for understanding quantum many-body dynamics, with deep connections to quantum computation.

title: Seven- And Eight-loop Critical Exponents Of The Three-dimensional Ising Model
authors: D. Shapoval, Yu. Honchar, B. Delamotte, M. Dudka, Yu. Holovatch
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the critical exponents [MATH], [MATH], and the correction-to-scaling exponent [MATH] of the three-dimensional Ising universality class by resumming the recently computed seven- and eight-loop renormalization-group series in the [MATH] expansion (O.~Schnetz, , 085018 (2018); O.~Schnetz, , 036002 (2023)). The resummation combines conformal mapping with a homographic transformation, while the resummation parameters are optimized according to two complementary criteria. This approach yields precise estimates of the critical exponents together with quantitative uncertainty estimates. We find that the error bar on [MATH] decreases rapidly with increasing loop order, whereas this is the case neither for [MATH] nor for [MATH]. Unexpectedly, although the estimated values are accurate in absolute terms, their slow convergence with the loop order leads to a slight but systematic tension with the conformal bootstrap estimates that are currently considered as the benchmark. We discuss several possible origins of this behavior and its implications for high-order resummations of perturbative renormalization-group series.
tldr: This paper computes critical exponents of the 3D Ising model using high-loop renormalization-group series, finding tension with conformal bootstrap results.
motivation: Accurate critical exponents are fundamental to statistical mechanics, and improving perturbative RG resummation methods is important for understanding phase transitions.
method: The authors resum seven- and eight-loop RG series in the epsilon expansion using conformal mapping and homographic transformation, optimizing parameters with two complementary criteria.
result: They obtain precise estimates for exponents nu, eta, and omega, but find that while nu's error bar shrinks with loop order, eta and omega converge slowly, leading to systematic tension with conformal bootstrap benchmarks.
conclusion: The results highlight limitations of high-order perturbative RG resummations for certain exponents and suggest the need for improved resummation techniques or alternative approaches.

title: A Sparse And Truncated State Vector Simulator For Peaked Circuits
authors: Diogo R. Ferreira
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a class of quantum circuits known as peaked circuits, the goal is to predict the most probable bit string at the output of the circuit. Since these circuits are designed to have a sharp peak in their output distribution, in principle it should be possible to simulate them using a truncated state vector with a limited number of terms, or a fraction of the total probability mass. This approximate simulation can be carried out on a classical computer with a sparse representation that stores only the nonzero amplitudes of the state vector, in contrast to the dense representations that are common in most quantum simulators. For efficiency, all operations on the state vector should be vectorized to the furthest possible extent and, if available, hardware acceleration can also be used. This work describes how these requirements were met in an open-source implementation, and discusses its performance and limitations.
tldr: This paper presents a classical simulator for peaked quantum circuits using sparse state vectors, focusing on computational efficiency rather than quantum information theory or thermodynamics.
motivation: Peaked circuits have output distributions with a sharp peak, making them amenable to approximate simulation with truncated state vectors, which could be more efficient than full simulation.
method: The simulator uses a sparse representation storing only nonzero amplitudes and vectorized operations, with optional hardware acceleration, to simulate peaked circuits classically.
result: The implementation demonstrates performance improvements for peaked circuits but has limitations in scalability and accuracy for circuits with broader distributions.
conclusion: The approach is useful for specific circuit classes but does not contribute to the core research directions of quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Kime-Representation Formulations Of Three Open Problems In The Foundations Of Classical Mechanics: Uncertainty, Invariant Entropy, And Directional Degrees Of Freedom
authors: Ivo D. Dinov
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give mathematically self-contained formulations, in the complex-time (kime) representation, of three open problems from the foundations of classical mechanics: (I) the extension of the classical entropic uncertainty principle to non-canonical variables and to multiple degrees of freedom; (II) the characterization of coordinate-invariant measures and entropies, i.e., the question of why continuous physical quantities must be paired for an invariant entropy to exist; and (III) the construction of a classical relativistic directional degree of freedom (a classical analogue of a spin-1/2 system). Throughout, the kime phase is interpreted {statistically as a latent circular random variable whose law \Phi models the intrinsic trial-to-trial variability of repeated, identically controlled experiments indexed by the kime magnitude. The mathematical bridge is an exact symplectic identification of the kime cone with the action-angle chart of a one-degree-of-freedom phase space, under which the kime measure is the Liouville measure and the phase law becomes the angular conditional of a Liouville density. Specifically, we (i) prove a sharp entropic uncertainty relation on the kime cylinder whose extremal family is von Mises x Gaussian, together with a sharp circular Fisher-information inequality saturated exactly by von Mises laws; (ii) prove an exact non-canonical uncertainty relation in which the correction term is the geometric mean of the Poisson bracket, clarifying the conjectured role of the expected bracket; (iii) prove aggregate multi-degree-of-freedom bounds via the Williamson normal form and Fischer's inequality, and isolate the per-degree-of-freedom refinement as a precise open problem of symplectic Schur-Horn type; (iv) prove that diffusion of the kime phase produces monotone entropy growth with the equipartitioned (Haar-uniform) phase law.
tldr: The paper formulates three open problems in classical mechanics using a complex-time (kime) representation, focusing on uncertainty, invariant entropy, and directional degrees of freedom.
motivation: To provide mathematically self-contained formulations of foundational problems in classical mechanics that have resisted resolution.
method: The author uses symplectic geometry and statistical modeling, interpreting the kime phase as a latent circular random variable, and derives uncertainty relations and entropy bounds.
result: Sharp entropic uncertainty relations on the kime cylinder, non-canonical uncertainty relations with Poisson bracket corrections, and multi-degree-of-freedom bounds via Williamson normal form.
conclusion: The kime representation offers a unified framework for addressing these classical problems, but the work is purely classical and does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Multi-agent Autoformalization Of Tensor Network Theory
authors: Sirui Lu, Erickson Tjoa, J. Ignacio Cirac
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We build a team of specialized large language-model agents and present an agent-driven workflow for research-level formalization in theoretical physics, with the autoformalization of the fundamental theorem of matrix-product states as a demonstration. The agents, coordinated through a structured mathematical blueprint and periodic human review, orchestrated and executed the full formalization autonomously. For some statements, the agents were able to explore new proof routes that are not part of the standard literature. Along the way the agents produced extensive tensor-network and quantum-information libraries not previously available in Mathlib, Lean's mathematical library. As a physical application, the formalization also extends towards symmetry-protected topological phases in one dimension. We find that the main bottleneck in large-scale autoformalization is enforcing mathematical intent and we provide a detailed study of the full process and various subtleties involved. We release the codebase as the library {TNLean}, together with a \nChapters{}-chapter {blueprint} of the formalization effort.
tldr: This paper uses multi-agent LLMs to autoformalize tensor network theory in Lean, demonstrating formalization of the fundamental theorem of matrix product states.
motivation: To automate the formalization of complex theoretical physics proofs, reducing human effort and exploring new proof routes.
method: A team of specialized LLM agents coordinated via a structured blueprint and periodic human review autonomously formalized tensor network theorems in Lean.
result: The agents successfully formalized the fundamental theorem of matrix product states, produced new tensor-network and quantum-information libraries for Mathlib, and extended formalization to symmetry-protected topological phases.
conclusion: Large-scale autoformalization is feasible but bottlenecked by enforcing mathematical intent; the approach can accelerate formal verification in theoretical physics.

title: Unveiling Semiclassical Structures In Quantum Chaotic Eigenstates Using Neural Networks
authors: J. Montes, F. Borondo, Gabriel G. Carlo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks and neural quantum states have consolidated a new paradigm to analyze and discover physical phenomena through constrained neural parametrizations. In this context, we investigate whether the semiclassical structure of the eigenfunctions of a quantum chaotic system can be unveiled through unsupervised learning. To this end, we train a "quantum dictionary", formulated as an overcomplete autoencoder, that sparsely represents the eigenstates of the system, using as an illustration the quantum baker map. The only explicit physical information imposed on the dictionary atoms is their localization in phase space, without providing any kind of information about the periodic orbits of the corresponding classical system. The model achieves high fidelity in reconstructing eigenstates not used during training. By comparing the learned atoms with an independently constructed "semiclassical dictionary", we find that they spontaneously localize on the periodic orbits and develop scar-like structures. This result is interesting in two ways: a localization constraint is sufficient to recover nontrivial semiclassical organization from spectral data and at the same time periodic orbits confirm their fundamental role in the structure of quantum chaotic eigenfunctions. More generally, our proposed architecture opens a new route to learning representations whose atoms optimize other chosen physical properties.
tldr: This paper uses neural networks to uncover semiclassical structures in quantum chaotic eigenstates, specifically scar-like features localized on periodic orbits.
motivation: Understanding the structure of quantum chaotic eigenfunctions is a fundamental problem; the authors aim to see if unsupervised learning can reveal semiclassical organization without prior knowledge of classical periodic orbits.
method: An overcomplete autoencoder (quantum dictionary) is trained on eigenstates of the quantum baker map, with a localization constraint in phase space, and the learned atoms are compared to a semiclassical dictionary.
result: The learned atoms spontaneously localize on periodic orbits and develop scar-like structures, achieving high reconstruction fidelity on unseen eigenstates.
conclusion: Localization constraints alone suffice to recover nontrivial semiclassical organization from spectral data, confirming the role of periodic orbits in quantum chaos.

title: Complex Spacing Ratio Statistics In The Partially Open Asymmetric Quantum Baker Map
authors: Leonardo Ermann, Pablo Sesin, Alejandro M. F. Rivas, Pablo D. Bergamasco, Gabriel G. Carlo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the complex eigenvalue statistics of the asymmetric quantum baker map with partial projective openings. The classical asymmetric baker map, with its discontinuity at [MATH], is fully chaotic, has no reflection symmetry, and provides a clean setting with tunable escape rate and fractal repeller dimension. We consider three distinct opening geometries in position space: localized (contiguous channels), random, and uniform (equispaced channels), all controlled by a tunable amplitude reflectivity parameter [MATH] that interpolates between the fully open ([MATH]) and the closed ([MATH]) limits. We use the partially truncated circular unitary ensemble (PTCUE) as the random matrix theory benchmark. The main focus is on the joint distribution of the complex spacing ratio [MATH], defined as the ratio of the distances from an eigenvalue to its nearest and next-nearest neighbors in the complex plane. We find a smooth crossover from a quasi-1D spectral regime, where eigenvalues cluster near the unit circle and the phase distribution of [MATH] is peaked, to a two-dimensional Ginibre-like regime, where the distribution becomes nearly uniform and level repulsion is fully developed. Both the number of open channels [MATH] and the reflectivity [MATH] modulate this crossover, and [MATH] provides an additional continuous control even at fixed opening size. All three opening models converge to PTCUE statistics at large [MATH], while differences are most pronounced for the localized model at small [MATH]. No evidence of an abrupt transition is found. This crossover which suggests a universal behavior, has deep consequences for open quantum and wave-chaotic experiments.
tldr: This paper studies complex spacing ratio statistics in the partially open asymmetric quantum baker map, focusing on spectral properties of open quantum systems.
motivation: To understand universal spectral features of open quantum chaotic systems with partial openings and tunable escape rates.
method: Numerical simulation of the asymmetric quantum baker map with three opening geometries and comparison to the partially truncated circular unitary ensemble (PTCUE) random matrix model.
result: A smooth crossover from quasi-1D to 2D Ginibre-like spectral statistics is observed, modulated by the number of open channels and reflectivity, with no abrupt transition.
conclusion: The crossover suggests universal behavior in open quantum systems, with implications for wave-chaotic experiments.

title: Dual-Platform Precision Measurement Of The $3^2d_{5/2}$ To $4^2s_{1/2}$ $g$-Factor Ratio In $^{40}\text{Ca}^+$
authors: Brian J. Mcmahon, Vikram S. Sandhu, John M. Gray, Creston D. Herold, Kenton R. Brown, Brian C. Sawyer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report precision measurements of the ratio of Land\'e [MATH] factors between the [MATH] and [MATH] states of a single trapped [MATH] ion. The measurements are performed in two distinct ion trap apparatus: a cryogenic surface electrode radiofrequency Paul trap and a room-temperature permanent magnet Penning trap. The Penning trap measurements yield a ratio of [MATH], which represents a more than 40-fold uncertainty reduction compared to previous work. The radiofrequency trap measurement yields a concurring value of [MATH]. We estimate that systematic shifts for each system are well below the respective statistical uncertainty.
tldr: Precision measurement of g-factor ratio in Ca+ ion using two different trap platforms.
motivation: To improve the precision of Landé g-factor ratio measurements for atomic state characterization.
method: Measurements performed in a cryogenic surface-electrode Paul trap and a room-temperature Penning trap, with systematic error analysis.
result: Penning trap measurement achieved a 40-fold uncertainty reduction; Paul trap measurement concurred.
conclusion: The dual-platform approach provides high-precision g-factor ratio values with well-characterized systematics.

title: Equilibrium In A Reaction Network Of Assemblies
authors: Germ\'an Kruszewski Giampaolo Folena
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a mean-field reaction network whose species are assemblies built from identical atoms by reversible coagulation and fragmentation. Each assembly is an ordered binary tree, so the number of species of a given length grows combinatorially, as the Catalan numbers. The model nonetheless admits an explicit equilibrium and tractable stochastic dynamics. A finite volume [MATH] sets a crossover length [MATH] that splits the equilibrium into two sectors. Below [MATH] each assembly occurs in many copies and the rank-frequency distribution is Zipf-like; above [MATH] individual species are rare and fluctuation-dominated. The statistical weight of the rare sector decays slowly with volume, controlling the finite-size scaling of diversity, Shannon entropy, and other assembly-weighted observables. The equilibrium also admits a transparent grand-canonical description in terms of a bond energy and an atomic chemical potential. Together these results make the model a controlled neutral baseline against which selection and driving in richer assembly networks can be measured.
tldr: This paper studies equilibrium properties of a reaction network of assemblies modeled as binary trees, focusing on statistical mechanics of assembly distributions.
motivation: To understand the equilibrium behavior of complex assembly networks and provide a neutral baseline for studying selection and driving.
method: A mean-field reaction network with reversible coagulation and fragmentation of binary tree assemblies is analyzed using equilibrium statistical mechanics and stochastic dynamics.
result: The model exhibits a crossover length splitting the equilibrium into a Zipf-like regime and a fluctuation-dominated regime, with explicit grand-canonical description.
conclusion: The model serves as a controlled neutral baseline for assembly networks, but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Associating Trajectories With Quantum Processes By Equivalent Spectra
authors: Elliott Tammaro, Sriram Gundla, Arunabh Pratik, Shyla Rathore
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum mechanics abandoned the classical notion of a particle trajectory, yet trajectories remain conceptually appealing for resolving foundational issues in quantum mechanics. Bohmian mechanics offers one route to associating trajectories with quantum processes, but it requires explicit non-locality to remain consistent with EPR-type experiments, placing it in tension with special relativity. We propose an alternative approach: rather than deriving trajectories from a quantum guidance equation, we search for classical trajectories whose radiated frequency spectra match those of quantum processes such as atomic transitions. Using the Li\'enard-Wiechert potentials, we compute the electric and magnetic fields generated by a point charge along a given trajectory, numerically solving the retarded-time and from these fields obtain the power spectrum of emitted radiation. By fitting the parameters of a chosen family of trajectories, we identify "equivalent spectrum" trajectories that reproduce a target frequency distribution, including ones of quantum mechanical origin. We discuss the implications of this method and propose future work to determine whether equivalent spectrum trajectories belong to a family governed by a differential equation, which would constitute a quantum-equivalent equation of motion.
tldr: This paper proposes associating classical trajectories with quantum processes by matching their radiated frequency spectra, using Liénard-Wiechert potentials to compute the power spectrum.
motivation: The authors aim to provide an alternative to Bohmian mechanics for associating trajectories with quantum processes, avoiding explicit non-locality and tension with special relativity.
method: They compute the electric and magnetic fields from a point charge along a chosen trajectory using Liénard-Wiechert potentials, solve the retarded-time equation numerically, and obtain the power spectrum of emitted radiation. They then fit trajectory parameters to match a target frequency distribution from quantum processes.
result: They identify 'equivalent spectrum' trajectories that reproduce the target frequency distribution, including those of quantum mechanical origin.
conclusion: The method shows promise for finding classical trajectories that mimic quantum spectra, and future work may determine if these trajectories obey a differential equation, potentially constituting a quantum-equivalent equation of motion.

title: A Quantum Reservoir Architecture For Chaotic Forecasting And A Test Of Whether Its High Dimension Helps
authors: Tushar Pandey
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computing uses a fixed quantum circuit as a feature generator and trains only a simple linear readout on top of it. This makes it cheap to train and free of the optimisation problems that affect many quantum machine-learning models. A natural worry is that the very large feature space the circuit produces might inflate apparent performance without adding anything real. This paper provides two things. First, it gives a complete, reproducible recipe for one such reservoir applied to forecasting chaotic systems, including how data is fed in, how the circuit is built, and how the readout is trained. Second, it gives a way to tell whether the reservoir's high dimension is actually doing useful work. We grow the size of the prediction problem and the size of the quantum reservoir together, so that extra capacity cannot be the explanation for any improvement, and we track a single stability number that measures how well behaved the readout fit is. On two chaotic test systems, a spatiotemporal chain and a shallow-water fluid model, the quantum reservoir keeps a flat, stable error as both sizes grow, while a matched classical reservoir does not. We report where the classical baseline is in fact stronger, so the comparison is honest. The result is a clean specification plus a diagnostic that other groups can apply to any reservoir whose features have a known scale.
tldr: A quantum reservoir computing architecture for chaotic forecasting with a diagnostic to test whether high dimensionality is beneficial.
motivation: Quantum reservoir computing is cheap to train but may inflate performance due to large feature space; the paper aims to provide a reproducible recipe and a diagnostic to assess whether high dimension actually helps.
method: The authors grow the prediction problem and quantum reservoir size together, tracking a stability number to measure readout fit, and compare against a matched classical reservoir on two chaotic systems.
result: The quantum reservoir maintains flat, stable error as both sizes grow, while the classical reservoir does not; the classical baseline is stronger in some cases.
conclusion: The quantum reservoir architecture is effective for chaotic forecasting, and the proposed diagnostic can be applied to other reservoirs with known feature scales.

title: Nuclear Many-Body Systems As Benchmarks For Quantum Computing
authors: Sota Yoshida, Alessandro Baroni, Takayuki Miyagi, Ermal Rrapaj
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a framework for benchmarking quantum algorithms for nuclear many-body systems based on realistic nuclear Hamiltonians such as chiral effective field theory. To this effect we introduce a workflow that maps nuclear interactions in second quantization formalism to qubit Hamiltonians. This enables the systematic construction of benchmark instances spanning no-core and valence-space formulations with two-body (NN) and selected three-body (3N) interactions. Then, we proceed to provide resource estimates for three representative eigenvalue algorithms: Quantum Phase Estimation, Quantum Krylov methods, and Observable Dynamic Mode Decomposition. We compare their resource requirements in terms of T-gate counts and system size, and examine the impact of model-space choices and many-body interactions. The primitives included in our analysis are Trotterization, Qubitization, and Quantum Singular Value Transformation. Our results quantify scaling trends across algorithms and problem classes, and provide a basis for consistent comparisons of quantum approaches to nuclear many-body problems. The implementation is provided by the NuQuLib software stack.
tldr: This paper benchmarks quantum algorithms for nuclear many-body problems using realistic Hamiltonians, focusing on resource estimation for eigenvalue algorithms.
motivation: To provide a framework for benchmarking quantum computing approaches to nuclear many-body systems, which is a specific application area not directly aligned with the user's research interests.
method: The authors map nuclear interactions to qubit Hamiltonians and compare Quantum Phase Estimation, Quantum Krylov methods, and Observable Dynamic Mode Decomposition in terms of T-gate counts and system size.
result: Quantified scaling trends across algorithms and problem classes, providing a basis for consistent comparisons of quantum approaches to nuclear many-body problems.
conclusion: The framework enables systematic benchmarking but is primarily relevant to quantum chemistry and nuclear physics, not the user's core directions.

title: Multiband Topological Group-velocity Control From Slow Light To Light Stopping
authors: Junhao Yang, Jiarui Wang, Jingyu Liu, Shirong Lin, Xinyuan Qi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) couplings into a Harper--Hofstadter photonic lattice to establish a long-range topological photonic platform for group-velocity engineering. We show that the NNN couplings not only open a previously closed band gap but also flatten the dispersion of the edge states, thereby offering a potential route toward topological slow-light control. Theoretical calculations reveal that the band gaps support band-gap Chern numbers with opposite signs. Propagation simulations demonstrate robust, topologically protected slow-light transport of counter-chiral edge states, while the presence of slow-light edge states in all three topological band gaps enables broadband topological slow light. By further tuning the NNN coupling parameter, multiple topological light-stopping states can be realized. These results establish long-range NNN coupling as an effective mechanism for topological group-velocity engineering and provide new design principles for topological slow-light devices, optical delay lines, and integrated multiband photonic systems.
tldr: This paper studies topological slow-light and light-stopping in a photonic lattice with next-nearest-neighbor couplings, focusing on group-velocity engineering.
motivation: To achieve broadband topological slow-light and light-stopping for applications in optical delay lines and integrated photonics.
method: Introduces next-nearest-neighbor couplings into a Harper-Hofstadter photonic lattice and analyzes band structure, Chern numbers, and edge state dispersion.
result: NNN couplings open band gaps, flatten edge state dispersion, and enable robust slow-light transport and multiple light-stopping states.
conclusion: Long-range NNN coupling is an effective mechanism for topological group-velocity engineering in photonic systems.

title: Equivariant Quantum Clustering With Differential Privacy: Parameter-Efficient Privacy-Preserving Analysis Across Heterogeneous Sensitive Datasets
authors: B. M. Taslimul Haq, Md Arifur Rahman, Tawfiq Al Islam Foysal, Abdullah Al Noman, Abir Ahmed
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy-preserving clustering is critical for analyzing sensitive data in healthcare, cybersecurity, and enterprise applications, where maintaining data confidentiality must be balanced with analytical performance. This paper presents Equivariant Quantum Clustering (EQC), a parameter-efficient framework that integrates symmetry-aware quantum circuits with differential privacy to improve the privacy-utility tradeoff. EQC employs p4m equivariant parameter sharing to reduce circuit complexity while preserving informative feature representations. The framework is evaluated on three privacy-sensitive datasets: NSL-KDD, CERT Insider Threat v6.2, and a synthetic MIMIC-III clinical dataset. On the NSL-KDD benchmark, EQC achieves 79.3% clustering accuracy while reducing membership inference attack success to 38.3% under a privacy budget of {\epsilon} = 1.0 and {\delta} = 10^-5, outperforming representative classical and quantum baselines. Ablation studies indicate that the performance gains primarily arise from parameter-efficient circuit design combined with differential privacy. The results demonstrate that EQC provides a practical quantum-ready framework for secure and privacy-preserving clustering across heterogeneous sensitive datasets.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum clustering framework with differential privacy, but it does not align with the user's research directions in quantum information theory, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Privacy-preserving clustering is important for sensitive data analysis, and the authors aim to improve the privacy-utility tradeoff using quantum circuits.
method: The framework uses p4m equivariant parameter sharing in quantum circuits combined with differential privacy to reduce circuit complexity and protect data.
result: On NSL-KDD, EQC achieves 79.3% clustering accuracy with membership inference attack success reduced to 38.3% under a privacy budget of epsilon=1.0.
conclusion: EQC provides a practical quantum-ready framework for secure clustering, but the contribution is primarily in applied machine learning and privacy, not in the user's core research areas.

title: Decomposition-Based Qaoa For Maximum Coverage Location Problem In Satellite Constellation Design
authors: Divya Sisodiya, Amiratabak Bahengam, Hang Woon Lee, Hao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An increase in earth observation missions has increased the demand of efficient design and optimization of satellite constellations. Maximizing coverage of the target while effectively utilizing the limited orbital resources is one of the critical design challenges for complex combinatorial optimization problems. The maximal covering location problem (MCLP), serves as a base for orbital coverage modeling, is NP-hard and computationally intractable for large-constellation instances. Using heuristics, metaheuristics, and mixed-integer linear programming, classical solvers have achieved optimal or near-optimal results, yet their scalability is limited as the problem size increases. Quantum computing advancements, including the quantum approximate optimization algorithms, offer a potential solution to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems. Current quantum hardware limitations, such as low qubit counts and circuit depth, restrict solutions for small-scale instance problems. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a scalable quantum optimization framework for MCLP in satellite constellation design. A decomposition-based quantum methodology is proposed, in which large MCLP instances are partitioned into subgraphs by classical decomposition, optimized independently via quantum optimization circuits, and combined using quantum reconstruction strategies. Computational results across different constellation sizes reveal better scalability in less time while maintaining competitive coverage performance compared to classical solvers.
tldr: This paper applies a decomposition-based quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to the maximum coverage location problem in satellite constellation design.
motivation: Satellite constellation design involves NP-hard combinatorial optimization; classical solvers face scalability issues, and current quantum hardware is limited to small instances.
method: The authors propose a scalable quantum optimization framework that partitions large MCLP instances into subgraphs using classical decomposition, optimizes each subgraph independently with QAOA, and combines them via quantum reconstruction strategies.
result: Computational results show better scalability in less time while maintaining competitive coverage performance compared to classical solvers.
conclusion: The decomposition-based QAOA approach offers a promising path to solving larger-scale satellite constellation optimization problems on near-term quantum devices.

title: Nyquist-Sampled Time-Domain Adjoint Fdtd For Memory-Efficient Broadband Nanophotonic Inverse Design
authors: Mingyu Park, Owen D. Miller, Haejun Chung
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adjoint optimization is a cornerstone of broadband nanophotonic inverse design, but conventional time-domain implementations face a severe memory bottleneck because they retain forward-field histories at every finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) time step. Here, we show that this full time-step storage is unnecessary for band-limited design objectives. By storing forward fields only at Nyquist-compliant temporal intervals and using the resulting sparse field history during the reverse-time adjoint pass, the proposed method enables on-the-fly gradient accumulation without retaining full forward- or adjoint-field histories. This Nyquist-sampled adjoint FDTD framework preserves the two-simulation scaling of time-domain adjoint optimization while substantially reducing the dominant field-storage cost. Gradient verification confirms that Nyquist-compliant sampling reproduces conventional full-storage adjoint gradients with negligible error, whereas undersampling beyond the Nyquist limit produces aliasing-induced gradient degradation. Across four two-dimensional broadband nanophotonic benchmarks and a fully three-dimensional metalens, the method maintains gradient fidelity and optimized device performance while reducing dominant field-storage memory by up to 107x. These results suggest that the principal memory barrier in broadband time-domain adjoint FDTD is not an intrinsic requirement of gradient evaluation, but a consequence of redundant temporal field storage, opening a practical route to large-scale three-dimensional nanophotonic inverse design.
tldr: A memory-efficient adjoint FDTD method for broadband nanophotonic inverse design using Nyquist sampling.
motivation: Conventional time-domain adjoint optimization suffers from a severe memory bottleneck due to storing forward fields at every FDTD time step, limiting scalability to large 3D problems.
method: Store forward fields only at Nyquist-compliant temporal intervals and use the sparse history during the reverse-time adjoint pass to compute gradients on-the-fly.
result: The method reduces field-storage memory by up to 107x while preserving gradient fidelity and optimized device performance across multiple benchmarks.
conclusion: The principal memory barrier in broadband time-domain adjoint FDTD is due to redundant temporal storage, and Nyquist sampling offers a practical route to large-scale 3D nanophotonic inverse design.

title: Efficient Pauli-decomposition And Multistage State-refinement For Tensor Network Based Differential Equation Solver
authors: Vishwabhushan Suresh Gholap, Himadri Shekhar Dhar, Siddhartha Santra
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical numerical techniques for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) become computationally expensive as the dimension of the discretized differential operator increases. For PDEs giving rise to Sturm--Liouville problems, tensor network (TN) methods can be highly productive: an operator of dimension [MATH] can be represented as a matrix product operator (MPO) using only [MATH] qubits, enabling computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors via imaginary time evolution (ITE). However, this remains computationally challenging. First, most methods for generating MPOs of large operators without explicit tensor-product structure require prohibitively large memory. Second, the number of Trotterization steps for convergence in conventional ITE increases rapidly with [MATH]. We present techniques to mitigate both challenges for certain sparse, structured differential operators. To address the first, we construct the MPO by expanding the operator in the Pauli-string basis, enabled by an analytical expression for the Pauli basis coefficients that reduces the memory requirement from [MATH] to [MATH]. To address the second, we propose a multistage state-refinement heuristic that accelerates ITE convergence, reducing convergence time by up to two orders of magnitude. Using this TN framework, we compute the first 32 eigenstates of a Laplacian of dimension exceeding [MATH] with fidelity above [MATH] using a 20-qubit MPO. We further validate the method on the 2D anharmonic oscillator and investigate disordered systems, where increasing random potential strength degrades accuracy and limits the approach.
tldr: This paper presents tensor network methods for solving partial differential equations, focusing on computational efficiency rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Classical PDE solvers become expensive for high-dimensional operators; tensor networks offer a compact representation but face memory and convergence challenges.
method: The authors construct matrix product operators via analytical Pauli decomposition and propose a multistage state-refinement heuristic to accelerate imaginary time evolution.
result: They compute eigenstates of a Laplacian of dimension over 2^100 with high fidelity using a 20-qubit MPO, and demonstrate the method on a 2D anharmonic oscillator and disordered systems.
conclusion: The techniques improve efficiency for sparse structured operators, but accuracy degrades for disordered systems, limiting applicability.

title: Learned Committors As Reaction Coordinates For Nucleation Rates
authors: David Quigley Hubert J. Naguszewski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central challenge in the analysis of first-order phase transitions is the identification of optimal reaction coordinates. In principle, the committor is the ideal choice; however, its computational cost has historically made it intractable. Here, we train a convolutional neural network ([MATH]-NN) as a proxy for the committor on brute-force committor labels and use it directly as the coordinate of a Markov state model. Applied to magnetisation reversal in the two-dimensional Ising model, [MATH]-NN reproduces brute-force nucleation rates across a range of thermodynamic conditions. The largest geometric cluster size also recovers accurate rates despite providing a poor pointwise predictor of the committor. These results demonstrate that an effective reaction coordinate for nucleation rate calculation must reliably separate the metastable and stable basins, but need not preserve the committor pointwise for every microstate. We stress that this distinction has direct implications for the choice of collective variable in rare-event simulations of nucleation more broadly.
tldr: This paper uses machine learning to find reaction coordinates for nucleation rates in the Ising model, focusing on classical phase transitions.
motivation: Identifying optimal reaction coordinates for first-order phase transitions is challenging; the committor is ideal but computationally expensive.
method: A convolutional neural network is trained as a proxy for the committor and used as the coordinate in a Markov state model to compute nucleation rates.
result: The neural network committor reproduces brute-force nucleation rates for magnetization reversal in the 2D Ising model; the largest geometric cluster size also yields accurate rates despite poor pointwise committor prediction.
conclusion: An effective reaction coordinate for nucleation rates must separate metastable and stable basins, but need not preserve the committor pointwise for every microstate.

title: Learning The Energy Landscapes Of Dynamical Systems Via Energetic Variational Optimal Transport Under Data Quantity--Quality Trade-offs
authors: Shun Wang, Chun Liu, Wenrui Hao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic optimal transport unifies optimal transport, fluid mechanics, and gradient-flow theory within a continuous dynamical framework, offering a geometry-aware language for applications across physics, biology, and machine learning. However, conventional formulations cast it as a constrained optimization problem that must explicitly satisfy the continuity equation, hindering the reconstruction of the underlying dynamics directly from data. We propose the energetic variational method for dynamic optimal transport (EVMDOT), which reformulates it within an energetic variational framework by combining the flow map, the least action principle, and the maximum dissipation principle. The flow map recasts the constrained problem as an unconstrained one by automatically enforcing the continuity equation, while the balance between the conservative and dissipative forces determines the velocity field. Applied to the Fokker--Planck equation, the EVMDOT reconstructs both the energy landscape and the Waddington landscape directly from time-series density data. Through numerical experiments, we reveal that the EVMDOT achieves an intrinsic balance between data quantity and data quality: a sufficient data quantity compensates for limited data quality, making the reconstruction robust to the choice of the observation window. We further apply the EVMDOT to the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset to infer the potential landscape of amyloid-[MATH] and tau, revealing two wells corresponding to the cognitively normal and Alzheimer's disease stages and the transition pathway between them.
tldr: This paper proposes an energetic variational method for dynamic optimal transport to learn energy landscapes from data, with applications to the Fokker-Planck equation and Alzheimer's disease data.
motivation: Conventional dynamic optimal transport formulations require explicit satisfaction of the continuity equation, hindering direct reconstruction of dynamics from data. The authors aim to reformulate it as an unconstrained problem using energetic variational principles.
method: The method combines the flow map, least action principle, and maximum dissipation principle to automatically enforce the continuity equation, and reconstructs the velocity field from the balance of conservative and dissipative forces.
result: Numerical experiments on the Fokker-Planck equation show that the method reconstructs energy landscapes robustly, with data quantity compensating for limited data quality. Application to ADNI data reveals two potential wells corresponding to cognitive normal and Alzheimer's stages.
conclusion: The proposed EVMDOT provides a data-driven approach to inferring energy landscapes of dynamical systems, demonstrating practical utility in biomedical data analysis.

title: Local Linear Convergence Of The Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient Method For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Xin Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Primal-dual first-order methods are widely used for large-scale semidefinite programming (SDP), but their ability to compute highly accurate solutions is not well explained by global convergence theory alone. We study the local convergence of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method applied to a standard primal--dual SDP pair. We show that PDHG converges eventually (R-)linearly whenever the limiting KKT point satisfies either strict complementarity or primal--dual nondegeneracy. The proof views PDHG as a preconditioned proximal point method for the KKT inclusion and combines its descent inequality with a local error bound. Under strict complementarity, the error bound follows from the local spectral geometry of the positive semidefinite cone; under primal-dual nondegeneracy, it follows from strong regularity of the KKT mapping. We also give a simple SDP instance where both regularity conditions fail and PDHG can converge only sublinearly. This contrasts with linear programming, where PDHG admits a local linear convergence regime even for degenerate instances. Numerical experiments support the theory and identify difficult SDP instances where PDHG struggles to reach high accuracy.
tldr: This paper analyzes the local linear convergence of the primal-dual hybrid gradient method for semidefinite programming, focusing on optimization theory rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding local convergence of first-order methods for SDP is important for large-scale optimization, but the paper does not connect to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.
method: The study views PDHG as a preconditioned proximal point method and uses error bounds under strict complementarity or primal-dual nondegeneracy.
result: PDHG converges R-linearly under either strict complementarity or primal-dual nondegeneracy, but sublinearly when both fail.
conclusion: The results provide theoretical insight into PDHG for SDP but are not relevant to the user's research interests in quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Multiuser Zak-OTFS On The Uplink With Superimposed Spread-Pilots
authors: Ananthanarayanan Chockalingam Sai Pradeep Muppaneni
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we consider the uplink of a multiuser Zak-OTFS system comprising users with heterogeneous delay-Doppler (DD) periods/frame sizes. Multiple access is achieved through time-frequency (TF) shifts that place the users in non-overlapping regions of the TF plane. Closed-form expressions for the effective DD domain channel between each user and the base station are derived for sinc and Gaussian pulse shaping filters. The inter-user interference (IUI) is shown to be negligible under the TF-shift-based multiple access, thereby decoupling the multiuser input-output relation (IOR) estimation problem into independent single-user estimation problems. For IOR estimation, a superimposed spread-pilot framework is employed. The spread-pilot sequence is obtained by applying FFT to a reshaped Zadoff-Chu sequence. To mitigate the pilot-data interference introduced by the superimposed spread-pilot, a DD dictionary-based IOR estimation scheme that iterates between IOR estimation and data detection is employed. Simulation results for a multiuser Zak-OTFS system demonstrate that the resulting IOR estimates achieve normalized mean-square error (NMSE) and bit error rate (BER) performances that closely match those of the corresponding single-user system. Furthermore, for sinc pulse shaping, the superimposed spread-pilot frame achieves higher spectral-efficiency compared to embedded pilot frame across a wide range of inter-user power ratios. For Gaussian pulse shaping, however, the embedded pilot frame achieves a higher spectral efficiency due to the combined effects of residual IUI and significant pilot-data interference in the case of superimposed spread-pilot. The robustness of the estimation framework to variations in channel power-delay profile and maximum Doppler shift is also demonstrated.
tldr: This paper proposes a multiuser Zak-OTFS uplink system with superimposed spread-pilots for channel estimation.
motivation: To enable multiple access in OTFS systems with heterogeneous users and improve spectral efficiency through efficient pilot design.
method: Uses TF-shift-based multiple access to decouple users, and a superimposed spread-pilot framework with FFT-reshaped Zadoff-Chu sequences for channel estimation, iterating between estimation and data detection.
result: The proposed scheme achieves NMSE and BER close to single-user performance; sinc pulse shaping yields higher spectral efficiency than embedded pilots, while Gaussian pulse shaping does not.
conclusion: The superimposed spread-pilot approach is effective for multiuser Zak-OTFS with sinc pulse shaping, but less so with Gaussian pulse shaping due to interference.

title: Braiding Structures On Categorical multi-Interval Jones-Wassermann Subfactor
authors: Yuze Ruan Zhengwei Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we construct braiding structures on the multi-interval Jones-Wassermann subfactor planar algebra associated with any unitary modular fusion category. Utilizing this construction, we provide a new proof of the self-duality of these subfactors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these braidings induce a projective unitary representation of the balanced superelliptic mapping class group; consequently, these structures effectively encode the non-trivial higher-genus data of the underlying category. As an application of this correspondence, we derive a generalized Verlinde formula as 2-box Fourier duality of the planar algebra.
tldr: This paper constructs braiding structures on multi-interval Jones-Wassermann subfactor planar algebras from unitary modular fusion categories, proving self-duality and deriving a generalized Verlinde formula.
motivation: To understand higher-genus data of modular fusion categories and provide a new proof of self-duality for these subfactors.
method: Using planar algebra techniques and categorical constructions to define braiding structures on multi-interval subfactors.
result: Braiding structures induce projective unitary representations of balanced superelliptic mapping class groups, and a generalized Verlinde formula is derived as 2-box Fourier duality.
conclusion: The work encodes non-trivial higher-genus categorical data and offers a new perspective on subfactor theory and modular categories.

title: A Reverse Riesz Estimate Combined With A Spectral Gap Implies A Poincar\'e Inequality
authors: C\'edric Arhancet
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Working at the level of an Abel-ergodic sectorial operator [MATH] on a Banach space [MATH] and an unbounded operator [MATH] defined on a subspace [MATH] in another Banach space [MATH], we show that a single reverse Riesz estimate [MATH] for some [MATH], combined with the condition [MATH], where [MATH] is the part of [MATH] on the closure of the range of [MATH], implies the Poincar\'e inequality [MATH], where [MATH] is the Abel-ergodic projection onto the kernel of [MATH]. The condition [MATH] is the natural abstract substitute for a spectral gap, and is sharp already in the Hilbertian case. We also obtain a companion divergence inequality. The arguments are remarkably short, yet the principle is genuinely unifying: it covers commutative and noncommutative situations on the same footing and can be used with arbitrary Banach spaces. As a consequence, we recover, and considerably extend, a recent theorem of Jiao, Luo, Zanin and Zhou [CMP2024] on (possibly noncommutative) [MATH]-spaces. We then illustrate the flexibility of the method across a wide spectrum of geometries, ranging from Riemannian manifolds, Lie groups, metric measure spaces, spin manifolds to genuinely noncommutative settings such as quantum groups, semigroups of Schur multipliers, [MATH]-Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups and quantum tori, where we sometimes establish new inequalities and otherwise recover classical ones from a single principle.
tldr: This paper proves a Poincaré inequality from a reverse Riesz estimate and a spectral gap condition in abstract Banach spaces, with applications to various geometric and noncommutative settings.
motivation: The authors aim to unify and extend known Poincaré inequalities across diverse mathematical structures using a single abstract principle.
method: They work with an Abel-ergodic sectorial operator on a Banach space and derive the inequality using a reverse Riesz estimate and a spectral gap condition, with short arguments.
result: The method recovers and extends a recent theorem on (noncommutative) Lp-spaces and yields new inequalities for Riemannian manifolds, Lie groups, quantum groups, etc.
conclusion: The principle is unifying and flexible, covering many geometries and noncommutative settings, but the paper is purely mathematical with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Why Constants Matter In Distribution Testing: From Uniformity To Calibration
authors: Alon Kipnis
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distribution goodness-of-fit testing has developed a powerful rate-level theory: we often know how the required sample size scales with the alphabet size, the separation from the null, and the target error probability. Uniformity testing is the canonical example. One can distinguish the uniform distribution on [MATH] categories from alternatives at total-variation distance at least [MATH] with far fewer than [MATH] samples, and the optimal scaling is now well understood. But rate-level theory leaves an important question unresolved: among several tests with the same sample-complexity order, which one actually gives the best risk or power? This is a constant-level question. It is especially relevant in modern applications where distribution testing is used not merely as an asymptotic abstraction, but as a practical design tool. This note argues that sharp constants in distribution testing play a role analogous to Fisher information in parametric estimation and Pinsker's constant in nonparametric estimation. First, they distinguish between tests that are all rate-optimal but not equally powerful. Second, they reveal the effective signal-to-noise ratio governing the testing problem. Third, they can guide tuning-parameter choices in downstream applications. We illustrate this perspective through large-alphabet uniformity testing and then explain why the same logic matters for choosing the number of bins in calibration testing.
tldr: This paper argues for the importance of sharp constants in distribution testing, using uniformity testing and calibration testing as examples.
motivation: Rate-level theory in distribution testing ignores constant factors, which matter for practical performance and tuning parameter selection.
method: The paper provides a perspective on why constants matter, drawing analogies to Fisher information and Pinsker's constant, and illustrates with large-alphabet uniformity testing and calibration testing.
result: Sharp constants distinguish between rate-optimal tests, reveal effective signal-to-noise ratios, and guide tuning-parameter choices.
conclusion: Constants are crucial for practical distribution testing, and the same logic applies to calibration testing.

title: Controllability And Exponential Mixing In Singular Interacting Particle Systems
authors: Laurent Mertz, Vahagn Nersesyan, Manuel Rissel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article concerns interacting particle systems with singular kernels, driven either by degenerate deterministic controls or by degenerate decomposable noise. In the deterministic setting, we establish global exact controllability and a topologically robust property called solid controllability. Moreover, we prove a result that guarantees global approximate controllability with prescribed trajectories. For stochastic dynamics, we obtain ergodicity and exponential mixing by utilizing coupling and recurrence mechanisms based on controllability. Our approach exploits the singularity and applies to a broad class of models, including Biot-Savart, Coulomb, Riesz, and Yukawa interactions, as well as heterogeneous multi-species systems.
tldr: This paper studies controllability and exponential mixing in interacting particle systems with singular kernels, using deterministic and stochastic control.
motivation: To understand controllability and ergodic properties of singular interacting particle systems, which are important in fluid dynamics and plasma physics.
method: The authors prove global exact controllability and solid controllability for deterministic systems, and establish ergodicity and exponential mixing for stochastic systems using coupling and recurrence mechanisms based on controllability.
result: They obtain global exact controllability, solid controllability, and global approximate controllability with prescribed trajectories for deterministic dynamics, and ergodicity with exponential mixing for stochastic dynamics.
conclusion: The singularity of interactions is exploited to achieve strong controllability and mixing properties, applicable to a broad class of models including Biot-Savart, Coulomb, Riesz, and Yukawa interactions.

title: Learning Ldpc Codes With Quantized Density Evolution Over Relaxed Protographs
authors: Gennady Shutkov, Dmitry Artemasov, Alexey Frolov, Pavel Rybin, Kirill Andreev
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the design of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes for a given iterative decoder. Despite tools such as direct simulation, density evolution (DE), and EXIT-chart analysis, selecting a parity-check matrix remains a difficult combinatorial optimization problem. Existing approaches often rely on population-based search, random mutations, genetic algorithms, or related heuristics, which require careful parameter tuning and may be computationally expensive. Recent gradient descent (GD)-based methods optimize relaxed parity-check matrices by differentiating through decoder simulations. However, such decoder-in-the-loop strategies rely on noisy Monte Carlo estimates, require line search over soft matrix representations, and remain costly for long LDPC codes. Moreover, although optimization is performed in a relaxed domain, the loss is typically evaluated only at integer-valued parity-check matrices. In this work, we focus on the design of long protograph-based LDPC codes and propose a deterministic GD-based framework that operates directly on a relaxed protograph representation. Each protograph entry is interpreted as the probability that the corresponding element is equal to one. The loss function is based on DE bit error rate (BER) performance and can be evaluated directly for relaxed protographs. To justify this relaxation, we associate the relaxed representation with an ensemble of binary protographs and show that the proposed relaxed DE gives the ensemble-averaged DE performance. The resulting optimization procedure is fully autonomous and uses standard GD methods. Owing to deterministic DE evaluation and informative gradients, the proposed approach provides fast and reliable convergence. Numerical experiments for the min-sum decoder show that the optimized protographs outperform 5G LDPC codes with the same protograph dimensions.
tldr: This paper proposes a gradient-descent-based method for designing LDPC codes using relaxed protographs and quantized density evolution.
motivation: Designing LDPC codes for iterative decoders is a combinatorial optimization problem; existing heuristic methods are computationally expensive and require careful tuning.
method: The authors interpret each protograph entry as a probability and use a deterministic gradient descent framework with a loss function based on density evolution bit error rate, evaluated directly on relaxed protographs.
result: The optimized protographs outperform 5G LDPC codes with the same protograph dimensions for the min-sum decoder.
conclusion: The proposed method provides fast and reliable convergence for designing long protograph-based LDPC codes without noisy Monte Carlo estimates.

title: Limits Of Uniform Certification In The Standard Turing Model -- Semantic Invariants And Admissible Methods
authors: Fabio F. G. Buono
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper does not address the mathematical truth of P versus NP. Instead, it identifies a structural limitation of uniform proof-generation methods in the standard Turing model. The observation is model-theoretic: it concerns the interaction between semantic invariants and syntactic verification, not the provability of complexity statements. We formalise an admissible method as a generator-verifier pair that produces, for each program, a finite certificate establishing a semantic property. Admissibility forces the generator-verifier composition to behave uniformly with respect to the invariant being certified. In the standard model, such uniform semantic certification implicitly induces a decision procedure for the property. Rice's theorem shows that this implicit behaviour cannot be realised for non-trivial semantic invariants, revealing a structural constraint on formal certification. Understanding this requires a meta-computational perspective: the obstruction arises from the computational behaviour induced by certification, not from the complexity-theoretic status of the property. We apply this framework to two semantic invariants naturally associated with formal certification of P vs. NP and with cryptographic hardness assumptions (in particular, one-way functions). Both fall under the same limitation: no uniform admissible method can certify them in the standard model. A complete Coq formalisation is provided, capturing the extensional structure of admissible methods and the semantic-syntactic interaction underlying the result.
tldr: This paper identifies a structural limitation of uniform proof-generation methods in the standard Turing model using model-theoretic arguments and a Coq formalization.
motivation: The paper aims to show that certain semantic properties, including those related to P vs NP and cryptographic hardness, cannot be certified by uniform admissible methods in the standard Turing model.
method: The author formalizes admissible methods as generator-verifier pairs and uses Rice's theorem to demonstrate that uniform semantic certification implicitly induces a decision procedure, which is impossible for non-trivial semantic invariants.
result: The paper proves that no uniform admissible method can certify the semantic invariants associated with P vs NP or one-way functions in the standard Turing model.
conclusion: The limitation is structural and model-theoretic, not complexity-theoretic, and applies to formal certification of certain semantic properties.

title: Degree-Constrained Interval Optimization For Minimax Polynomial Approximation In Homomorphic Encryption
authors: Jiheon Woo, Donggyun Ryu, Yongjune Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables privacy-preserving inference under arithmetic constraints that restrict encrypted evaluation to additions and multiplications. As a result, non-polynomial activation functions must be replaced by polynomial approximations. Among polynomial approximation methods, minimax approximation, typically computed by the Remez algorithm, is a standard approach because it minimizes the maximum approximation error over a given design interval. For minimax polynomial design, the approximation interval is a critical hyperparameter: a wider interval improves robustness to large-magnitude inputs while increasing the minimax approximation error under a fixed degree budget. In this paper, we formulate this trade-off as a distribution-aware interval optimization problem, where the approximation interval is chosen to minimize the mean-squared error (MSE) with respect to the pre-activation distribution of interest. To effectively control outside-interval inputs, we combine minimax polynomials with domain extension functions (DEFs) and their HE-realizable polynomial counterparts, domain extension polynomials (DEPs), which approximate a clipping operation outside the design interval and thereby suppress uncontrolled polynomial extrapolation. We first derive an analytically tractable DEF-based proxy objective that captures the trade-off between within-interval minimax approximation error and outside-interval clipping error. We then connect this idealized objective to HE-realizable DEP constructions through an implementation-error decomposition with an accompanying upper bound.
tldr: This paper proposes a degree-constrained interval optimization method for minimax polynomial approximation in homomorphic encryption, focusing on privacy-preserving inference.
motivation: Homomorphic encryption requires polynomial approximations of non-polynomial functions, and the choice of approximation interval critically affects accuracy and robustness.
method: The authors formulate a distribution-aware interval optimization problem to minimize mean-squared error, and combine minimax polynomials with domain extension functions to control outside-interval inputs.
result: They derive an analytically tractable proxy objective and connect it to HE-realizable polynomial constructions via an implementation-error decomposition.
conclusion: The proposed method improves the trade-off between approximation error and input robustness for polynomial approximations in HE.

title: Locality Of Curve-Decoding And Improved Proximity Gaps
authors: Rohan Goyal, Venkatesan Guruswami, Yihang Sun, Mary Wootters
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proximity gaps are a property of error correcting codes that arise in the study of Interactive Oracle Proofs (IOPs) and Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Zero Knowledge (SNARKs). Recent work of Goyal and Guruswami has established near-optimal proximity gaps for many families of codes, including subspace design codes, as well as random ensembles like random linear codes, Reed-Solomon codes with random evaluation points, and Gallager's ensemble of LDPC codes (Goyal & Guruswami, 2025). However, the parameters for these latter randomized ensembles are worse than the parameters for subspace design codes, and degrade as the degree ell increases. In this work, we obtain improved proximity gaps for random ensembles of codes, including random linear codes, Reed-Solomon codes with random evaluation points, and Gallager's ensemble. Quantitatively, our results for these random ensembles match the results that Goyal and Guruswami attained for subspace design codes. In fact, our techniques are a black-box transference from subspace design codes: any progress on subspace design codes will automatically lead to analogous progress for these random ensembles. To obtain our results, we extend the Local Coordinate-wise Linear (LCL) property framework developed by Levi, Mosheiff, and Shagrithaya and by Brakensiek, Chen, Dhar, and Zhang to a version (Levi, Mosheiff & Shagrithaya, 2025; Brakensiek, Chen, Dhar & Zhang, 2025). This allows us to cast -- a property that implies proximity gaps -- directly as a row-span constrained LCL property, and make use of that machinery. In contrast, because curve-decodability is not obviously a vanilla LCL property, prior work had worked with a proxy property instead, leading to the aforementioned parameter losses.
tldr: This paper improves proximity gaps for random code ensembles by extending the LCL property framework to curve-decodability.
motivation: Proximity gaps are crucial for IOPs and SNARKs, but prior results for random codes had worse parameters than subspace design codes.
method: The authors extend the Local Coordinate-wise Linear (LCL) property framework to cast curve-decodability as a row-span constrained LCL property, enabling a black-box transfer from subspace design codes.
result: They achieve proximity gaps for random linear codes, Reed-Solomon codes, and Gallager's LDPC codes that match the best known parameters for subspace design codes.
conclusion: The work provides a general technique to transfer proximity gap results from subspace design codes to random code ensembles, improving their applicability in cryptographic proofs.

title: On The Convergence Of Belief Propagation For Multipath Data Association In Target Tracking
authors: Kuilong Yang, Zengfu Wang, Hua Lan, Jing Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Belief propagation (BP) is widely used for data association (DA) in target tracking. Existing convergence analyses of BP for DA address only the two-way correspondence between targets and measurements, where each target generates at most one measurement per scan. Multipath DA (MPDA) allows a single target to produce multiple measurements via distinct propagation paths, creating a three-way correspondence among targets, paths, and measurements, for which a complete convergence proof has not yet been provided. We provide such a proof for the BP updates in MPDA, establishing convergence to a unique fixed point. Simulations illustrate the convergence behavior of BP in MPDA and demonstrate a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off relative to both single-scan and two-scan variants of the multiple-detection multiple-hypothesis tracker.
tldr: This paper proves convergence of belief propagation for multipath data association in target tracking, a classical multi-target tracking problem.
motivation: Existing convergence analyses of BP for data association only cover two-way correspondence; multipath DA involves three-way correspondence and lacks a convergence proof.
method: The authors provide a convergence proof for BP updates in multipath DA by formulating the problem as a factor graph and showing the BP iterations converge to a unique fixed point.
result: Simulations demonstrate convergence behavior and a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared to multiple-detection multiple-hypothesis trackers.
conclusion: BP for multipath DA converges to a unique fixed point, enabling efficient and accurate tracking in scenarios with multiple detections per target.

title: Achieving Unanimous Consensus Through Multi-Agent Deliberation
authors: Apurba Pokharel, Ram Dantu, Shakila Zaman, Vinh Quach, Sirisha Talapuru
abstract: ArXiv:2504.02128v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Blockchain consensus mechanisms have relied on algorithms such as Proof-of-Work (PoW) and Proof-of-Stake (PoS) to ensure network functionality and integrity. However, these approaches struggle with adaptability for decision-making where the opinions of each matter rather than reaching an agreement based on honest majority or weighted consensus. This paper introduces a novel deliberation-based consensus mechanism where Large Language Models (LLMs) act as rational agents engaging in structured discussions to reach a unanimous consensus. By leveraging graded consensus and a multi-round deliberation process, our approach ensures unanimous consensus for definitive problems and graded consensus for prioritized decision problems and policies. We provide a formalization of our system and use it to show that the properties of blockchains are maintained, while also addressing the behavior in terms of adversaries, stalled deliberations, and confidence in consensus. Moreover, experimental results demonstrate system feasibility, showcasing convergence, block properties, and accuracy, which enable deliberative decision-making on blockchain networks.
tldr: This paper proposes a blockchain consensus mechanism using LLM agents to achieve unanimous or graded consensus through structured deliberation.
motivation: Traditional blockchain consensus mechanisms like PoW and PoS lack adaptability for opinion-based decision-making where each participant's view matters.
method: The authors design a multi-round deliberation process where LLM agents discuss and update their positions, using graded consensus to reach agreement.
result: Experimental results show feasibility, convergence, block properties, and accuracy, demonstrating deliberative decision-making on blockchain networks.
conclusion: The proposed deliberation-based consensus mechanism maintains blockchain properties while enabling more flexible consensus for decision-making problems.

conclusion: The work provides insights into the connection between matrix models and string theory, but is not directly applicable to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Unified First-Principles Formula For Time-Resolved Arpes Spectra Of Coherent And Incoherent Excitons Beyond The Dilute Limit

Despite major experimental progresses in time-resolved and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, a quantitative, microscopic framework for interpreting exciton-induced modifications of electronic band structures—applicable even beyond the low-density limit—is still lacking. Here, we close this …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 026402] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a first-principles formula for time-resolved ARPES spectra of excitons beyond the dilute limit.
motivation: A quantitative microscopic framework for interpreting exciton-induced band structure modifications in time-resolved ARPES is lacking, especially beyond the low-density limit.
method: The authors derive a unified formula based on many-body perturbation theory, incorporating both coherent and incoherent exciton contributions.
result: The formula captures excitonic effects in photoemission spectra and is applicable beyond the dilute limit, enabling analysis of high-density exciton systems.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical tool for interpreting time-resolved ARPES experiments on excitonic materials, bridging a gap between theory and experiment.

conclusion: This work provides a practical mechanism for realizing broadband flat bands in photonic systems, with potential applications in light confinement and nonlinear optics.

authors: Yaqing Han, Siqi Jiang, Jingkuan Xiao, Jiawei Jiang, Yulu Liu, Jiabei Huang, Yu Du, Di Zhang, Fuzhuo Lian, Wanting Xu, Siqin Wang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Xiaoxiang Xi, Alexander S. Mayorov, Renjun Du, Kai Chang, Hongxin Yang, Lei Wang, And Geliang Yu

authors: Seong-Ho Shinn, Matteo Massaro, Mithun Thudiyangal, And Adolfo Del Campo

[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 020402] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes generating spontaneous quantum turbulence in a Bose-Einstein condensate via the Kibble-Zurek mechanism during a thermal quench.
motivation: To explore the formation of topological defects and quantum turbulence in a controlled quantum system, linking phase transition dynamics to turbulent behavior.
method: Numerical simulations of Bose-Einstein condensation driven by a thermal quench, analyzing defect formation and vortex dynamics.
result: Spontaneous quantum turbulence is observed, characterized by a tangle of quantized vortices, arising from the Kibble-Zurek mechanism.

title: Maximum Entropy Conjecture For Black Hole Mergers
authors: Monica Rincon-Ramirez, Nathan K. Johnson-Mcdaniel, Eugenio Bianchi, Ish Gupta, Vaishak Prasad, And B. S. Sathyaprakash
abstract:

tldr: The paper proposes a maximum entropy conjecture for black hole mergers, suggesting that the merged remnant behaves like a Kerr black hole.
motivation: To understand the final state of black hole mergers and whether entropy bounds govern the process.
method: Theoretical analysis using general relativity and black hole thermodynamics, comparing entropy of the initial binary system to that of a single Kerr black hole.
result: The authors find that the entropy of the merged remnant is consistent with the maximum entropy bound, supporting the conjecture.
conclusion: The maximum entropy conjecture may provide a simple description of black hole merger remnants, but further tests are needed.

title: Realization Of Floquet-Engineered Topological Complex-Energy Band Braids In Single-Photon Interferometry

motivation: To explore exotic nonequilibrium topological phenomena beyond static systems using Floquet engineering.

conclusion: This work provides a new approach to generating OAM-carrying microwave beams, with potential for high-capacity communications and radar.

title: Superconductivity From Phonon-Mediated Retardation In A Single-Flavor Metal
authors: Yang-Zhi Chou, Jihang Zhu, Jay D. Sau, And Sankar Das Sarma

tldr: This paper studies phonon-mediated superconductivity in a single-flavor metal with Berry curvature, focusing on retardation effects.
motivation: To understand how Berry curvature and retardation affect phonon-mediated pairing and superconductivity.
method: The authors analyze a model of a single-flavor metal with tunable Berry curvature, comparing static BCS approximation with full retardation effects.
result: They find that retardation alone can induce d-wave superconductivity even without Berry curvature, and Berry curvature can further modify the pairing.
conclusion: Retardation effects are crucial for unconventional superconductivity in single-flavor metals, and Berry curvature provides additional tunability.

method: Renormalization-group analysis of quantum metric and Berry curvature in quasicrystal models.
result: Discovery of a universal mechanism for divergent enhancement of quantum geometric quantities.
conclusion: Quantum geometry in quasicrystals exhibits hierarchical structures with universal scaling behavior.

result: They demonstrate the emergence of the 3D superconformal Ising critical point with the expected critical exponents and operator spectrum.
conclusion: The fuzzy sphere method is a viable tool for studying supersymmetric CFTs, opening new avenues for nonperturbative investigations.
